Let us read it for you. Listen now. Your browser does not support the audio element. Sy Gomberg, who headed the documentary branch of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences at the time, visited Hot Springs in 1991. Like so many other visitors to the Spa City through the decades, he fell in love with the place. Gomberg urged business and civic leaders to start a documentary film festival. "In 1992, a small group of arts enthusiasts in the area initiated the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival," writes historian Nancy Hendricks. "A special attraction that year was award-winning actor James Whitmore. Ten documentary films that had been nominated for Academy Awards were shown with Whitmore commenting that Hot Springs could be 'the documentary capital of the world.' "By 1993, the number of entries quadrupled, with 44 documentary films being screened. Actor James Earl Jones was featured that year at a fundraising gala and stated: 'I see the 1990s as holding the promise of an unparalleled era of popularity for nonfiction film and video with the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival as one of the genre's most important venues.' "In 1994, more than 5,000 people attended the festival. Several dozen films were screened, and 14 documentary filmmakers were present. They met with the audience, answered questions and took part in discussions about their work." The country had a president who had grown up in Hot Springs, and the folks there were enjoying the national attention. The Malco Theatre on Central Avenue was acquired in 1996 to serve as the festival's home. The theater had opened in 1935. It was built in the shell of the Princess Theatre, a vaudeville venue. The Art Deco structure was added to the National Register of Historic Places in January 2010. The theater was frequented by President Bill Clinton when he was a boy. "The economy of Hot Springs depended on lodging, dining and entertainment to support its burgeoning tourism industry," Hendricks writes. "In the late 1800s, Hot Springs attracted visitors from across the country to take the waters. After their therapeutic bathing, visitors sought amusements and recreation. At first this was limited to hunting, fishing and horseback riding. The demand increased for diversions such as gambling and entertainment." An opera house opened on Central Avenue in 1882 to host traveling companies. Frank Head, the opera house manager, commissioned construction of the Princess in 1910 for vaudeville shows and silent movies. It was built where Bridge Street connects Broadway to Central. Sidney Nutt Sr. bought the Princess in 1927 and converted it to sound in 1929. "Hot Springs' downtown business district suffered a number of catastrophic fires in the early 1900s," Hendricks writes. "The Princess survived until Christmas Eve 1935, when a blaze destroyed all but its foundation and it masonry entrance on Broadway. Those elements became the cornerstone of the Malco. Working with the architectural firm Brueggeman & Swaim to utilize the shell of the Princess, Nutt rebuilt it after the fire. "When complete, the irregularly shaped theater had a large auditorium, balcony, lobby and area for offices facing Central Avenue. The front of the theater included striking Art Deco elements that were popular at the time. In 1936, Nutt sold his interest in the Princess to M.A. Lightman of Memphis, founder of the Malco Theatre group. The Princess was renamed the Malco with the name incorporating Lightman's initials." The theater was renovated in 1946, the year the number of people coming to Hot Springs to take the baths peaked. Including its orchestra pit and balcony, there were more than 1,000 seats. "It was considered a showplace of the South, boasting the finest projection and sound equipment," Hendricks writes. "From 1929 until 1964, entrances were segregated. The entrance for Blacks was on Broadway. The white entrance was on Central. ... With advances in the civil rights movement in the 1960s, segregation of entrances and seating arrangements ended. During the Cold War, the building's heavy steel beams and 14-inch concrete walls led to the Malco being declared a bomb shelter." The Malco was renovated in 1962. As soon as I became old enough to drive in 1975, I began making Saturday trips from my home in Arkadelphia to the Malco so I could spend the afternoons watching movies. When the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival took over the theater, the plan was for there to be activities throughout the year. As is the case with so many nonprofit organizations, however, the festival ran into financial troubles and was forced to sell the building in 2013 in order to retire its debts. The festival moved up the street to the Arlington Hotel. Real estate developer Rick Williams purchased the Malco. In 2017, magician Maxwell Blade renovated the theater and made it the home of his shows. Blade continued to perform there until his retirement earlier this year. Though it has had its ups and downs, the festival hangs on. In 1997, Hot Springs was a stop on the Library of Congress' Film Preservation Tour, which featured films from the National Film Registry. The tour was designed to bring noteworthy movies to big screens throughout the country while promoting awareness of the need for film preservation. The Hot Springs event was attended by the president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. "While the festival is truly international in nature, it also serves to spotlight its home state of Arkansas," Hendricks writes. "Featured films have included a documentary about Glen Campbell, a film by documentarian Pam Maus on women in politics such as Arkansas' Hattie Caraway, a feature about the Marshallese community in Arkansas, and the critically acclaimed 'Command and Control' about the 1980 Titan II missile explosion near Damascus." Celebrity guests who have attended the festival through the years include Ed Asner, Beau Bridges, Eleanor Coppola, Peter Coyote, Allen Ginsberg, Louis Gossett Jr., Tess Harper, Tippi Hedren, Diane Ladd, Connie Stevens, George Takei and Kathleen Turner. In 2016, the Hot Springs Documentary Film Institute's archives were moved to the University of Arkansas at Fayetteville. The archives include extensive film holdings along with photographs and other memorabilia. During the pandemic, documentaries were screened through a virtual platform. There was also a drive-in series at a mall in Hot Springs. In 2022, the Brent Renaud Career Achievement Award was created to honor Renaud, an Arkansan who was the first foreign journalist killed following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. He was killed by Russian soldiers on March 13, 2022. "In 2023, the festival expanded its offerings to include such events as student field trips and classroom visits by filmmakers," Hendricks writes. "An emerging filmmaker program in collaboration with Arkansas PBS was designed for middle and high school students who were invited to take part in workshops. In partnership with a filmmaking program at Low Key Arts in Hot Springs, the festival hosted a 12-week documentary boot camp in which participants produced, directed and edited short documentaries to be showcased at the festival." This year's festival took place Oct. 10-18. Ken Jacobson now serves as the HSDFI executive director. Annie Gerber is the programming manager, and Molly Wheat is the festival producer. Oaklawn was this year's presenting sponsor. Special events were held at the start and end of the festival at Oaklawn's event center. Most screenings remained at the Arlington. There were special screenings at Hot Springs Village and National Park College. Nightly parties took place at venues such as Deluca's and the Superior Bathhouse Brewery. Jon Alpert, winner of 17 National Emmy Awards, was the 2025 recipient of the Renaud Career Achievement Award. Sy Gomberg, who headed the documentary branch of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences at the time, visited Hot Springs in 1991. Like so many other visitors to the Spa City through the decades, he fell in love with the place. Gomberg urged business and civic leaders to start a documentary film festival. "In 1992, a small group of arts enthusiasts in the area initiated the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival," writes historian Nancy Hendricks. "A special attraction that year was award-winning actor James Whitmore. Ten documentary films that had been nominated for Academy Awards were shown with Whitmore commenting that Hot Springs could be 'the documentary capital of the world. ' "By 1993, the number of entries quadrupled, with 44 documentary films being screened. Actor James Earl Jones was featured that year at a fundraising gala and stated: 'I see the 1990s as holding the promise of an unparalleled era of popularity for nonfiction film and video with the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival as one of the genre's most important venues. ' "In 1994, more than 5,000 people attended the festival. Several dozen films were screened, and 14 documentary filmmakers were present. They met with the audience, answered questions and took part in discussions about their work. " The country had a president who had grown up in Hot Springs, and the folks there were enjoying the national attention. The Malco Theatre on Central Avenue was acquired in 1996 to serve as the festival's home. The theater had opened in 1935. It was built in the shell of the Princess Theatre, a vaudeville venue. The Art Deco structure was added to the National Register of Historic Places in January 2010. The theater was frequented by President Bill Clinton when he was a boy. "The economy of Hot Springs depended on lodging, dining and entertainment to support its burgeoning tourism industry," Hendricks writes. "In the late 1800s, Hot Springs attracted visitors from across the country to take the waters. After their therapeutic bathing, visitors sought amusements and recreation. At first this was limited to hunting, fishing and horseback riding. The demand increased for diversions such as gambling and entertainment. " An opera house opened on Central Avenue in 1882 to host traveling companies. Frank Head, the opera house manager, commissioned construction of the Princess in 1910 for vaudeville shows and silent movies. It was built where Bridge Street connects Broadway to Central. bought the Princess in 1927 and converted it to sound in 1929. "Hot Springs' downtown business district suffered a number of catastrophic fires in the early 1900s," Hendricks writes. "The Princess survived until Christmas Eve 1935, when a blaze destroyed all but its foundation and it masonry entrance on Broadway. Those elements became the cornerstone of the Malco. Working with the architectural firm Brueggeman & Swaim to utilize the shell of the Princess, Nutt rebuilt it after the fire. "When complete, the irregularly shaped theater had a large auditorium, balcony, lobby and area for offices facing Central Avenue. The front of the theater included striking Art Deco elements that were popular at the time. In 1936, Nutt sold his interest in the Princess to M. Lightman of Memphis, founder of the Malco Theatre group. The Princess was renamed the Malco with the name incorporating Lightman's initials. " The theater was renovated in 1946, the year the number of people coming to Hot Springs to take the baths peaked. Including its orchestra pit and balcony, there were more than 1,000 seats. "It was considered a showplace of the South, boasting the finest projection and sound equipment," Hendricks writes. "From 1929 until 1964, entrances were segregated. The entrance for Blacks was on Broadway. The white entrance was on Central. With advances in the civil rights movement in the 1960s, segregation of entrances and seating arrangements ended. During the Cold War, the building's heavy steel beams and 14-inch concrete walls led to the Malco being declared a bomb shelter. " The Malco was renovated in 1962. As soon as I became old enough to drive in 1975, I began making Saturday trips from my home in Arkadelphia to the Malco so I could spend the afternoons watching movies. When the Hot Springs Documentary Film Festival took over the theater, the plan was for there to be activities throughout the year. As is the case with so many nonprofit organizations, however, the festival ran into financial troubles and was forced to sell the building in 2013 in order to retire its debts. The festival moved up the street to the Arlington Hotel. Real estate developer Rick Williams purchased the Malco. In 2017, magician Maxwell Blade renovated the theater and made it the home of his shows. Blade continued to perform there until his retirement earlier this year. Though it has had its ups and downs, the festival hangs on. In 1997, Hot Springs was a stop on the Library of Congress' Film Preservation Tour, which featured films from the National Film Registry. The tour was designed to bring noteworthy movies to big screens throughout the country while promoting awareness of the need for film preservation. The Hot Springs event was attended by the president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. "While the festival is truly international in nature, it also serves to spotlight its home state of Arkansas," Hendricks writes. "Featured films have included a documentary about Glen Campbell, a film by documentarian Pam Maus on women in politics such as Arkansas' Hattie Caraway, a feature about the Marshallese community in Arkansas, and the critically acclaimed 'Command and Control' about the 1980 Titan II missile explosion near Damascus. " Celebrity guests who have attended the festival through the years include Ed Asner, Beau Bridges, Eleanor Coppola, Peter Coyote, Allen Ginsberg, Louis Gossett Jr. , Tess Harper, Tippi Hedren, Diane Ladd, Connie Stevens, George Takei and Kathleen Turner. In 2016, the Hot Springs Documentary Film Institute's archives were moved to the University of Arkansas at Fayetteville. The archives include extensive film holdings along with photographs and other memorabilia. During the pandemic, documentaries were screened through a virtual platform. There was also a drive-in series at a mall in Hot Springs. In 2022, the Brent Renaud Career Achievement Award was created to honor Renaud, an Arkansan who was the first foreign journalist killed following Russia's invasion of Ukraine. He was killed by Russian soldiers on March 13, 2022. "In 2023, the festival expanded its offerings to include such events as student field trips and classroom visits by filmmakers," Hendricks writes. "An emerging filmmaker program in collaboration with Arkansas PBS was designed for middle and high school students who were invited to take part in workshops. A top-notch political thriller, The Diplomat stars Keri Russell as Kate Wyler, a newly appointed United States Ambassador to the United Kingdom who must manage numerous international crises in addition to her turbulent personal life. Through three seasons, The Diplomat has delivered riveting drama as Russell’s character negotiates with government officials and struggles in her marriage to former U.S. ambassador Hal Wyler (Rufus Sewell). Now more than ever, fans of the Netflix series should take the time to watch Russell’s best show: a political thriller with many similar qualities to The Diplomat . Videos by ComicBook.com Russell headlined FX’s The Americans from 2013 to 2018, portraying Elizabeth Jennings, a Russian KGB officer who leads a double life with her fellow spy and husband Philip Jennings (Matthew Rhys) in 1980s Washington D.C. A winner of four Emmy awards, the spy thriller brilliantly doubles as a family drama over the course of its six seasons. The Americans has earned widespread critical acclaim, and now is the perfect moment for fans of The Diplomat to discover this exceptional TV show. Read Next 10 Best Dramas to Binge on Netflix Right Now The Americans Is a Genuine TV Masterpiece Image Courtesy of FX Over a decade ago, The Americans rose to prominence thanks to its gripping suspense and compelling drama. Hiding in plain sight proves to be a challenging and perilous task for Philip and Elizabeth, as their undercover work in the U.S. frequently endangers their lives and threatens to compromise their secrecy. The pair’s high-stakes missions test their morality and allegiance to their country, leading to numerous surprising twists and shocking outcomes. In addition to The Americans ‘ intense spy plot, the show impressively spotlights Philip and Elizabeth’s family life. Their two children initially aren’t aware of their parents’ double lives, and Philip and Elizabeth’s efforts to keep their family together amid their unconventional circumstances make for a fascinating story arc. Outside of Philip and Elizabeth, The Americans features many more interesting characters in the U.S. government and the KGB. The Jenningses’ FBI agent neighbor, Stan Beeman (Noah Emmerich), serves as a friendly adversary for the main characters, while various Soviet embassy officials and KGB handlers play a significant role in the narrative. The Americans paints an intricate portrait of tensions during the Cold War’s later years from both a personal and a broad perspective. Regarded as one of the best period drama series of all time, The Americans explores its setting’s political climate and develops characters with incredible poise. Fans of The Diplomat Will Love The Americans Image Courtesy of Netflix Anyone who enjoys The Diplomat ‘s blend of international politics and interpersonal drama will be enthralled by The Americans . Kate Wyler’s personal turmoil involving her unstable marriage in The Diplomat somewhat mirrors the obstacles Philip and Elizabeth Jennings face in The Americans . Moreover, conflicts between nations play a pivotal part in both shows. As intense thrillers with a strong focus on family and relationships, the two shows deliver captivating plot threads that easily keep viewers hooked. All in all, The Diplomat ‘s story doesn’t quite stack up to The Americans ‘ meticulous buildup and satisfying payoffs. So, fans of the outstanding Netflix series have to stream The Americans . The Americans is available to stream on Hulu. What do you think? text: Deadline Print Article deadline-logo-svg Print Nana Mensah Upped To Series Regular On Netflix’s ‘The Diplomat’ For Season 4 By Rosy Cordero , Katie Campione November 4, 2025 2:06pm Nana Mensah; 'The Diplomat Stephanie Diani/Netflix EXCLUSIVE: Nana Mensah has been promoted to series regular for Season 4 of Netflix’s hit political drama The Diplomat . Mensah has been with the show since Season 1 as the tenacious and extremely loyal White House Chief of Staff Billie Appiah, who has become much more involved in the story over the course of three seasons as the President of the United States has evolved from an opaque character to a key figure in U.S. Ambassador Kate Wyler’s (Keri Russell) investigation into the bombing of a British aircraft carrier in the Persian Gulf. In Season 3, Billie must ingratiate herself with newly minted POTUS Grace Penn (Allison Janney)— the very woman she’d been back channeling to oust as VP. Mensah is a Ghanaian-American writer, director, actor and producer. She wrote, directed, and stars in the feature Queen of Glory, which premiered at the Tribeca Film Festival in 2021, where it won Best New Narrative Director. The film was also nominated for two Indie Spirit Awards for Best First Feature. On TV, Mensah starred in Presumed Innocent for Apple alongside Jake Gyllenhaal. She also recently played the series regular role of Yaz in Netflix’s The Chair opposite Sandra Oh. In addition to writing and acting, Mensah has also performed on Broadway in “Jaja’s African Braiding” and “Fear of 13” at the Donmar Warehouse opposite Adrien Brody. Mensah is represented by WME, 3 Arts Entertainment, Independent Talent Group, and Hansen, Jacobson, and Teller. The first show is the romantic comedy Nobody Wants This starring Kristen Bell and Adam Brody . We’ve also got the Keri Russell political drama The Diplomat, along with The Witcher, whose new season is the first since star Henry Cavill’s exit. The romantic comedy series was nominated in three major categories on TV’s biggest night, which took place at the Peacock Theater in Los Angeles on Sunday, September 14. Adam Brody received his first-ever Emmy nod in the […] ‘Nobody Wants This’ (2024-Present) In this touching dramedy, Kristen Bell stars as Joanne — a sex positive agnostic who co-hosts a podcast about sex and dating with her sister Morgan (Succession ‘s Justine Lupe ). Joanne unexpectedly falls for Noah Roklov (Adam Brody), a rabbi whom she’s introduced to through friends. Despite the culture clash of their dueling beliefs, Joanne and Noah try to make their relationship work despite vastly different lives and families. Nobody Wants This was highly praised by critics for its tackling of interfaith relationships in addition to its humor and fantastic chemistry between Bell and Brody. Season 2, which was just released on Netflix on October 23, also received positive reviews. It still manages to be sharp, insightful and emotionally resonant. ‘The Diplomat’ (2023-Present) The initial premise of The Diplomat centers on career United States diplomat Kate Wyler (Keri Russell), who has just been appointed the US ambassador to the United Kingdom. Immediately plunged into the midst of an international crisis she has to defuse, Kate must balance strategic alliances while she adjusts to her new high-profile job. At the same time, her marriage to fellow diplomat Hal Wyler ( Rufus Sewell ) flounders as he struggles with a lack of posting while his wife takes the spotlight. While The Diplomat initially received generally positive reviews for its first and second seasons, many critics have felt that the recent third season has been the show’s best. Amping up the political intrigue, character chemistry, emotional stakes and top-notch performances, The Diplomat’s third season establishes it as a wildly entertaining slice of melodrama. Thank You! Image via Netflix By Justine Kraemer Published Nov 1, 2025 Justine Kraemer is a Senior List Writer at Collider and a freelance writer based in Ontario, Canada. She is passionate about finding new angles on the latest movies and TV shows. With over five years of industry experience, her goal is to highlight lesser-known and interesting elements of pop culture projects. Sign in to your Collider account follow Follow followed Followed Like Like Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Political thrillers often serve as a mirror to real-world power dynamics, offering both entertainment and commentary. For fans of the edge-of-your-seat storytelling featured in A House of Dynamite , there are series that offer a treasure trove of series that explore similar themes, providing endless suspense long after the credits roll. Like A House of Dynamite , these shows excel at building multi-layered characters who navigate treacherous landscapes of ambition, betrayal, and corruption . For fans of the movie A House of Dynamite , the thrill of high-stakes political crises and morally complex decisions doesn't have to end with the movie's closing credits. For viewers who found that adrenaline-fueled experience left them wanting more, political thriller series offer stories that expand on these themes over multiple episodes, and sometimes seasons. The best political thriller series like A House of Dynamite introduce ordinary characters who navigate often unimaginable circumstances . 1 'Designated Survivor' (2016–2019) Tom Kirkman (Kiefer Sutherland) addresses the nation in Designated Survivor. Image via ABC Designated Survivor introduces Tom Kirkman ( Kiefer Sutherland ), a low-level U.S. Cabinet member who unexpectedly becomes President after a catastrophic attack kills the President and most of Congress during the State of the Union address. The series follows Kirkman as he's thrust into the role with no preparation, and how he navigates intense political pressure, national security crises, and personal struggles while trying to rebuild the government and uncover the truth behind the attack. For those who appreciate how A House of Dynamite presents a high-stakes political and military crisis, Designated Survivor offers a similar feel . A House of Dynamite and Designated Survivor focus on procedural, strategic-thinking, "inside the room" kind of tension. At their core, both stories are about the search for truth in the face of chaos . Both are often hard to watch since they ask viewers to think about unimaginable worst-case scenarios. 2 'Occupied' (2015–2020) Still from "Occupied". Image via TV2 Occupied is a Norwegian series that's set in a near future where Norway halts its oil and gas production to combat climate change, triggering an energy crisis in Europe. In response, the European Union, with Russia's help, orchestrates a "soft" occupation of Norway to restore oil output. The series follows Prime Minister Jesper Berg ( Henrik Mestad ) and ordinary citizens as they navigate the blurred lines between cooperation and resistance under foreign control. A House of Dynamite and Occupied present stories that both feel alarmingly plausible since they are set against the backdrop of modern geopolitical tension. In A House of Dynamite , the suspense centers on how leaders and citizens react to an immediate existential threat. Occupied extends that same energy into a long-form political thriller, where Norway faces a form of Russian occupation. Both stories are about real-world ethical dilemmas, and the fragility of national sovereignty . 3 'The Bureau' (2015–2020) Malotru (Mathieu Kassovitz) outdoors looking to the side with a bag strap over his shoulder in The Bureau. Image via Canal+ The Bureau is a French espionage drama that follows the inner workings of France's Directorate-General for External Security (DGSE). The series specifically focuses on intelligence officers who live under deep cover abroad. The story centers on Guillaume Debailly ( Mathieu Kassovitz ), code name "Malotru," a top agent who returns to Paris after six years undercover in Syria and struggles to readjust while secretly reconnecting with his former lover, endangering himself and the agency. For those who appreciate the realism in A House of Dynamite , The Bureau offers a similar kind of story . A House of Dynamite captures the pressure, secrecy, and moral tension that come with crisis decision-making, and T he Bureau takes those same qualities and develops them over several seasons . While A House of Dynamite shows the immediate chaos and urgency of a national security emergency, The Bureau dives into the long game of espionage and how agents manipulate information. 4 'Borgen' (2010–2022) Sidse Babett Knudsen as Birgitte, Freja Riemann as Laura, Emil Poulson as Magnus and Mikael Birkkjaer as Philip in Borgen. Image via DR1 Borgen is a Danish drama that follows Birgitte Nyborg ( Sidse Babett Knudsen ), a principled and ambitious politician who unexpectedly becomes Denmark's first female Prime Minister. The series explores the personal and professional challenges she faces as she tries to balance idealism with the compromises of power , navigate coalition politics, and maintain her family life amid constant media scrutiny. Fans of A House of Dynamite should watch Borgen because both explore the intersection of politics, power, and personal morality under extreme pressure. While A House of Dynamite thrusts leaders into an immediate national crisis where every decision carries explosive consequences, Borgen examines those same pressures in a more sustained, realistic political setting. For those drawn to A House of Dynamite for its tension and focus on decision-making under duress, Borgen expands on those themes . 5 'Paradise' (2025–) Paradise is set in the years following a catastrophic event and takes place in a city-sized underground bunker in Colorado. The series specifically follows United States Secret Service Agent Xavier Collins ( Sterling K. Brown ), who is under suspicion for the murder of the President of the United States . Paradise sees Collins do everything he can to uncover the truth and figure out who he can trust. A House of Dynamite and Paradise both explore the chaos and moral ambiguity of political crises, and how these bring out the best and worst of humanity. While A House of Dynamite follows a crisis unfolding in real time, and Paradise takes place in the aftermath of such a catastrophe , both spotlight how quickly truth can become a casualty of chaos. These stories explore how loyalty, power, and truth shift in moments when democracy and humanity hang by a thread. 6 'Scandal' (2012–2018) Kerry Washington as Olivia Pope handing Tony Goldwyn as Fitzgerald Grant a drink in the Oval Office in Scandal. Image via ABC Scandal introduces Olivia Pope ( Kerry Washington ), a brilliant crisis management expert in Washington, D.C., who dedicates her life to protecting the public images of the nation's elite while hiding explosive secrets of her own . She leads a team of "gladiators" who handle political scandals, criminal cover-ups, and personal crises with ruthless efficiency. Scandal follows Pope as she navigates complex relationships , particularly with U.S. President Fitzgerald Grant ( Tony Goldwyn ). For those who appreciate how A House of Dynamite explores how corrupting power can be, especially in a crisis, Scandal does the same . While A House of Dynamite captures the intensity of a national emergency and the decisions leaders must make in moments of chaos, Scandal extends that same adrenaline-fueled atmosphere into the ongoing world of Washington, D.C. politics. These stories explore the fragility of truth and integrity, particularly in moments of crisis. ​​​​​​ 7 'House of Cards' (2013–2018) Robin Wright in her office in House of Cards. Image via Netflix House of Cards introduces Frank Underwood ( Kevin Spacey ), a ruthless American Congressman who will stop at nothing to achieve power in Washington, D.C. After being passed over for a promised cabinet position, Underwood orchestrates a complex web of manipulation, betrayal, and political maneuvering to climb the ranks , with his equally ambitious wife, Claire ( Robin Wright ), by his side. House of Cards then follows Claire as she consolidates power for herself. For those who appreciate the fact that A House of Dynamite shows that, even in the midst of a crisis, leadership takes a toll on those who make critical decisions, House of Cards offers a deep dive into this idea. House of Cards takes a broader view of how political maneuvering is simply part of the process . A House of Dynamite hooks viewers with suspense, ethical gray zones, and intense political scenarios, and House of Cards offers a serialized look at how power is wielded and defended. 8 'Chernobyl' (2019) Boris (Stellan Skarsgård) and Valery (Jared Harris) stand outside in 'Chernobyl.' Image via HBO Chernobyl is a historical miniseries that chronicles the catastrophic nuclear disaster that occurred at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in 1986 in the Soviet Union. The series begins by showing the catastrophic explosion itself, and then breaks down the consequences that followed. Chernobyl is mainly told from the perspective of Valery Legasov ( Jared Harris ), a Soviet scientist who fought tirelessly to fight against the censorship that kept the truth from coming out. Both A House of Dynamite and Chernobyl are deeply human stories that don't sugarcoat the threats society faces . In A House of Dynamite , the tension comes from an immediate national emergency, forcing leaders and ordinary citizens to act under intense pressure. Similarly, Chernobyl portrays a real-life catastrophe, showing how individuals, including scientists and first responders, faced impossible choices in the midst of systemic failure and bureaucratic obstruction. 9 'The Diplomat' (2023–) Keri Russell and Rufus Swell sit in chairs next to each other in a large room in a scene from The Diplomat. Image via Netflix The Diplomat is a sharp, high-stakes political thriller centered on Kate Wyler ( Keri Russell ), a veteran U.S. diplomat unexpectedly appointed as Ambassador to the United Kingdom at a moment of escalating international crisis. In her role, she has to juggle complex foreign policy maneuvers, alliances and covert operations while dealing with the difficulties in her personal life, including the strain on her marriage to former diplomat Hal ( Rufus Sewell ). While A House of Dynamite focuses on a fictional national crisis and The Diplomat looks at the challenges of international relations , both stories examine the fact that anyone working in these roles faces impossible decisions every day . Both stories highlight the intersection of public duty and private morality, showing how leaders and negotiators balance ethical choices, personal relationships, and professional obligations under extreme pressure. 10 'The Americans' (2013–2018) Elizabeth (Keri Russell) and Phillip Jennings (Matthew Rhys) looking pensive in 'The Americans'. Image via FX The Americans is an espionage drama set during the Cold War in the 1980s, focusing on Elizabeth (Keri Russell) and Philip Jennings ( Matthew Rhys ), two Soviet KGB officers living undercover as a seemingly ordinary American married couple in suburban Washington, D.C. While maintaining their domestic charade, they carry out covert missions against the U.S. government , balancing loyalty to their country with the challenges of raising children who are unaware of their true identities. Both A House of Dynamite and The Americans focus on the human cost of operating in extreme situations . For those who were drawn to A House of Dynamite for the way it handles the tension between duty and conscience, The Americans offers a long-form exploration of the same themes. The Americans provides a suspenseful experience like A House of Dynamite , emphasizing the peril, strategy, and moral gray zones inherent in lives defined by crisis and secrecy. Both are often hard to watch since they ask viewers to think about unimaginable worst-case scenarios. 2 'Occupied' (2015–2020) Still from "Occupied". Image via TV2 Occupied is a Norwegian series that's set in a near future where Norway halts its oil and gas production to combat climate change, triggering an energy crisis in Europe. In response, the European Union, with Russia's help, orchestrates a "soft" occupation of Norway to restore oil output. The series follows Prime Minister Jesper Berg ( Henrik Mestad ) and ordinary citizens as they navigate the blurred lines between cooperation and resistance under foreign control. A House of Dynamite and Occupied present stories that both feel alarmingly plausible since they are set against the backdrop of modern geopolitical tension. In A House of Dynamite , the suspense centers on how leaders and citizens react to an immediate existential threat. Occupied extends that same energy into a long-form political thriller, where Norway faces a form of Russian occupation. Both stories are about real-world ethical dilemmas, and the fragility of national sovereignty. 3 'The Bureau' (2015–2020) Malotru (Mathieu Kassovitz) outdoors looking to the side with a bag strap over his shoulder in The Bureau. Image via Canal+ The Bureau is a French espionage drama that follows the inner workings of France's Directorate-General for External Security (DGSE). The series specifically focuses on intelligence officers who live under deep cover abroad. The story centers on Guillaume Debailly ( Mathieu Kassovitz ), code name "Malotru," a top agent who returns to Paris after six years undercover in Syria and struggles to readjust while secretly reconnecting with his former lover, endangering himself and the agency. For those who appreciate the realism in A House of Dynamite , The Bureau offers a similar kind of story. A House of Dynamite captures the pressure, secrecy, and moral tension that come with crisis decision-making, and T he Bureau takes those same qualities and develops them over several seasons. While A House of Dynamite shows the immediate chaos and urgency of a national security emergency, The Bureau dives into the long game of espionage and how agents manipulate information. 4 'Borgen' (2010–2022) Sidse Babett Knudsen as Birgitte, Freja Riemann as Laura, Emil Poulson as Magnus and Mikael Birkkjaer as Philip in Borgen. Image via DR1 Borgen is a Danish drama that follows Birgitte Nyborg ( Sidse Babett Knudsen ), a principled and ambitious politician who unexpectedly becomes Denmark's first female Prime Minister. The series explores the personal and professional challenges she faces as she tries to balance idealism with the compromises of power , navigate coalition politics, and maintain her family life amid constant media scrutiny. Fans of A House of Dynamite should watch Borgen because both explore the intersection of politics, power, and personal morality under extreme pressure. While A House of Dynamite thrusts leaders into an immediate national crisis where every decision carries explosive consequences, Borgen examines those same pressures in a more sustained, realistic political setting. For those drawn to A House of Dynamite for its tension and focus on decision-making under duress, Borgen expands on those themes. 5 'Paradise' (2025–) Paradise is set in the years following a catastrophic event and takes place in a city-sized underground bunker in Colorado. The series specifically follows United States Secret Service Agent Xavier Collins ( Sterling K. Brown ), who is under suspicion for the murder of the President of the United States. Paradise sees Collins do everything he can to uncover the truth and figure out who he can trust. A House of Dynamite and Paradise both explore the chaos and moral ambiguity of political crises, and how these bring out the best and worst of humanity. While A House of Dynamite follows a crisis unfolding in real time, and Paradise takes place in the aftermath of such a catastrophe , both spotlight how quickly truth can become a casualty of chaos. These stories explore how loyalty, power, and truth shift in moments when democracy and humanity hang by a thread. 6 'Scandal' (2012–2018) Kerry Washington as Olivia Pope handing Tony Goldwyn as Fitzgerald Grant a drink in the Oval Office in Scandal. Image via ABC Scandal introduces Olivia Pope ( Kerry Washington ), a brilliant crisis management expert in Washington, D. , who dedicates her life to protecting the public images of the nation's elite while hiding explosive secrets of her own. She leads a team of "gladiators" who handle political scandals, criminal cover-ups, and personal crises with ruthless efficiency. Scandal follows Pope as she navigates complex relationships , particularly with U. President Fitzgerald Grant ( Tony Goldwyn ). For those who appreciate how A House of Dynamite explores how corrupting power can be, especially in a crisis, Scandal does the same. While A House of Dynamite captures the intensity of a national emergency and the decisions leaders must make in moments of chaos, Scandal extends that same adrenaline-fueled atmosphere into the ongoing world of Washington, D. These stories explore the fragility of truth and integrity, particularly in moments of crisis. ​​​​​​ 7 'House of Cards' (2013–2018) Robin Wright in her office in House of Cards. Image via Netflix House of Cards introduces Frank Underwood ( Kevin Spacey ), a ruthless American Congressman who will stop at nothing to achieve power in Washington, D. After being passed over for a promised cabinet position, Underwood orchestrates a complex web of manipulation, betrayal, and political maneuvering to climb the ranks , with his equally ambitious wife, Claire ( Robin Wright ), by his side. House of Cards then follows Claire as she consolidates power for herself. For those who appreciate the fact that A House of Dynamite shows that, even in the midst of a crisis, leadership takes a toll on those who make critical decisions, House of Cards offers a deep dive into this idea. House of Cards takes a broader view of how political maneuvering is simply part of the process. A House of Dynamite hooks viewers with suspense, ethical gray zones, and intense political scenarios, and House of Cards offers a serialized look at how power is wielded and defended. 8 'Chernobyl' (2019) Boris (Stellan Skarsgård) and Valery (Jared Harris) stand outside in 'Chernobyl. ' Image via HBO Chernobyl is a historical miniseries that chronicles the catastrophic nuclear disaster that occurred at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant in 1986 in the Soviet Union. The series begins by showing the catastrophic explosion itself, and then breaks down the consequences that followed. Chernobyl is mainly told from the perspective of Valery Legasov ( Jared Harris ), a Soviet scientist who fought tirelessly to fight against the censorship that kept the truth from coming out. Both A House of Dynamite and Chernobyl are deeply human stories that don't sugarcoat the threats society faces. In A House of Dynamite , the tension comes from an immediate national emergency, forcing leaders and ordinary citizens to act under intense pressure. Similarly, Chernobyl portrays a real-life catastrophe, showing how individuals, including scientists and first responders, faced impossible choices in the midst of systemic failure and bureaucratic obstruction. 9 'The Diplomat' (2023–) Keri Russell and Rufus Swell sit in chairs next to each other in a large room in a scene from The Diplomat. Image via Netflix The Diplomat is a sharp, high-stakes political thriller centered on Kate Wyler ( Keri Russell ), a veteran U. diplomat unexpectedly appointed as Ambassador to the United Kingdom at a moment of escalating international crisis. In her role, she has to juggle complex foreign policy maneuvers, alliances and covert operations while dealing with the difficulties in her personal life, including the strain on her marriage to former diplomat Hal ( Rufus Sewell ). While A House of Dynamite focuses on a fictional national crisis and The Diplomat looks at the challenges of international relations , both stories examine the fact that anyone working in these roles faces impossible decisions every day. Both stories highlight the intersection of public duty and private morality, showing how leaders and negotiators balance ethical choices, personal relationships, and professional obligations under extreme pressure. 10 'The Americans' (2013–2018) Elizabeth (Keri Russell) and Phillip Jennings (Matthew Rhys) looking pensive in 'The Americans'. Image via FX The Americans is an espionage drama set during the Cold War in the 1980s, focusing on Elizabeth (Keri Russell) and Philip Jennings ( Matthew Rhys ), two Soviet KGB officers living undercover as a seemingly ordinary American married couple in suburban Washington, D. While maintaining their domestic charade, they carry out covert missions against the U. government , balancing loyalty to their country with the challenges of raising children who are unaware of their true identities. Both A House of Dynamite and The Americans focus on the human cost of operating in extreme situations. For those who were drawn to A House of Dynamite for the way it handles the tension between duty and conscience, The Americans offers a long-form exploration of the same themes. The Americans provides a suspenseful experience like A House of Dynamite , emphasizing the peril, strategy, and moral gray zones inherent in lives defined by crisis and secrecy. 'Slender Man' attacker found Terrifyingly, Netflix's The Diplomat just predicted EXACTLY Russia's new underwater nuke Chris Longridge Fri, October 31, 2025 at 2:04 PM UTC 2 min read The Diplomat correctly predicted Russia's new nuke Netflix Yesterday (Thursday 30 Oct), Vladimir Putin was crowing about the latest military technology that Russia has developed to defend itself against whatever threats Vladimir Putin perceives in the wider world. So far, so business-as-usual for the rest of us just trying to manage day-our to-day anxiety levels in the 21st century. The hardware in question is an underwater, nuclear-powered drone. A driverless nuclear submarine, if you will, with the capability of delivering a nuclear warhead that would create a radioactive tsunami. It sounds like something out of James Bond, really. Or Netflix's The Diplomat. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Because as it happens, the Macguffin in the current series of The Diplomat, airing on Netflix now, is just that: a nuclear-powered underwater drone. The "doomsday-level' item is being carried by a Russian submarine off the coast of the UK, and kickstarts a political crisis as the US and UK realise Russia is capable of destroying coastal cities and raining radioactive fallout over their nations' seaboards. US Ambassador to the UK Keri Russell, POTUS Alison Janney and PM Rory Kinnear all get their international relations in a twist over what to do about it. Netflix In the (fictional) show, the device is called Poseidon, after the Greek god of the sea. In real life, Putin's drone is called Poseidon, after the Greek god of terrifying ironic coincidences. Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement Advertisement We are not kidding: Both The Diplomat and the Russian mililtary-industrial complex decided at the same time to invent an underwater nuclear-powered drone with warhead capabilities and an identical purpose, and they both called it Poseidon. We're not suggesting for a moment that the writers of The Diplomat have access to intelligence reports deep inside Russia and used their stolen knowledge to warn the world about the dangers inherent in such a device. Nor are we suggesting they're psychic. We're just saying it's a really frightening coincidence, and that we should all pay very close attention in future to what The Diplomat says about world events because this one, frankly, was far too close to the mark for our comfort. Image via Netflix By Jessica Nobleza Published Nov 2, 2025 Jessica is a young writer from Brisbane, Australia. An avid consumer and lover of all things Film and TV, you will never tear her away from a screen. A tendency rooted from childhood, she once had dreams of becoming a member of the famed kids-band 'Hi-5'. Perhaps that's what pushed her to secure an education with a theater background. But now, as dreams evolved, her passions have turned to admiring performances from afar. Frankly, she's just grateful that she can put her binging skills to good use. Outside of work, Jessica recently completed her undergraduate double degree in Arts/Communications at the University of Queensland. Other than that, she spends most of her free time with family and friends, probably never forgetting to talk about the new movie or show she watched the day prior. Sign in to your Collider account Summary Generate a summary of this story follow Follow followed Followed Like Like Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Season 3 of The Diplomat didn't just raise the stakes — it detonated them. Indeed, the show pushed its characters to their limits, unraveling marriages, alliances, and the illusion that diplomacy is ever truly noble. What began as one of the best political dramas has since grown into an even better psychological thriller, one where every deal hides a secret agenda and every handshake could start a war. That's the beauty of a show that seamlessly blends the personal with the geopolitical. And sure, while it may be some time before our burning questions are finally answered in the next season, why not take the time to celebrate the genius we have just witnessed? So, from unexpected deaths to a final twist that rewrites everything we thought we knew, here are the moments in The Diplomat 's third season that dropped our jaws to the floor. 7 Margaret Roylin Dies Margaret Roylin (Celia Imrie) looking smug Image via Netflix. Having been exposed as one of the architects of the HMS Courageous' attack — a strike that resulted in the mass death of her own people — Margaret Roylin ( Celia Imrie ) spends much of the show cornered by her own political manipulations (and guilt). That is, until the early moments of Season 3, when she takes her own life while in CIA custody. It's an unsettling early shock, particularly because her suicide abruptly cuts off any hope of accountability. And frankly speaking, what makes the moment so jarring isn't just the death itself, but the power vacuum it leaves behind. Roylin was the loose thread that symbolized how deep the political deception really went. She was the perfect scapegoat for the US, and her loss signals a shift from crisis management to cover-up control — especially in the case of Eidra Park ( Ali Ahn ), London's CIA station chief, who must scramble to somehow protect her job (and herself) from becoming the sacrificial lamb. 6 Kate Stays in London as Ambassador Keri Russell as Kate sitting in the back of a limo with Rufus Sewell as her husband Hal in The Diplomat Season 3 Image via Netflix When Hal ( Rufus Sewell ) is selected as the next Vice President, Kate ( Keri Russell ) faces the difficult decision to follow him to Washington and leave her position in London — despite some encouraging her to find a compromise. Sadly for Hal, Kate proves she'd rather live an ocean away from her husband and stay in London as the Ambassador, declaring, in essence, that she's a diplomat first and a wife second. The decision hits like a gut punch, quietly reasserting her independence even as it signals the disintegration of her marriage. Indeed, the scene's brilliance lies in its understatement. There's no explosive argument nor any grand speech: just a simple shot of their faces as Kate remains stoic and still, not following her husband on the plane. It's shocking precisely because it seems so final. Both come to the realization that Kate's devotion to her career outweighs her willingness to play the supporting role of "Second Lady," as she is not one for performative action. 5 Kate Takes a Lover or Two(ish) Kerri Russell as Kate Wyler with David Gyasi as Dennison standing across from each other in The Diplomat. Image via Netflix For a character who prides herself on professionalism, Kate's romantic entanglements this season pushed her dangerously close to the edge. Her chemistry with Britain's Foreign Secretary Austin Dennison ( David Gyasi ) reaches a breaking point, with the two finally acting on their attraction and engaging in a moment of passion in the secrecy of his office. Sadly, it quickly fizzled off-screen and was left unresolved. Cut to an episode later, and audiences meet British spy Callum Ellis ( Aidan Turner ), whose profession is just as dangerous as his fiery affair with Kate. What's shocking isn't simply that Kate allows intimacy — she's human, after all — but that she does so amid the highest stakes of her career. Yes, she may be separated from her husband, but the world doesn't know about that. And sadly, as Second Lady, she must live up to certain reputational expectations. In many ways, these dalliances reveal her vulnerability, and in a world of alliances and betrayals, the heart may be the greatest liability of all. 4 President Rayburn Is Blamed for Britain’s Warship Attack Michael McKean as President Rayburn and Rufus Sewell as Hal Wyler in "The Diplomat' Image via Netflix Just when it seems the truth about the HMS Courageous attack will finally surface, the White House (prompted by Kate herself) makes a stunning move to shift the blame onto the late President William Rayburn ( Michael McKean ). It's a strategic deflection meant to shield Grace Penn's ( Allison Janney ) new administration from scandal, but the choice reeks of moral decay. Because who weaponizes a dead man's reputation? For those who served under Rayburn, such as the likes of Billie ( Nana Mensah ) and Stuart ( Ato Essandoh ), the choice is devastating. The man who once embodied steady, ethical leadership is turned into a villain overnight. It's a moment that perfectly captures the show's view of modern diplomacy, where optics trump truth and loyalty is little more than a narrative convenience. 3 Trowbridge Goes Rogue at the Press Conference President Grace Penn (Allison Janney) and Prime Minister Nichol Trowbridge (Rory Kinnear) stand on a podium while giving a joint press-conference. Penn's head is turned to her left, looking at Trowbridge. Image via Netflix. Hoping to contain the scandal and diplomatically close the book on the HMS Courageous crisis, the US and UK governments are set to deliver an agreed-upon statement that would share the blame for the attack. Unfortunately, things don't go to plan, as Britain's government is led by the most unpredictable politician of all time. Indeed, while standing at the podium next to President Grace Penn, Prime Minister Nichol Trowbridge ( Rory Kinnear ) completely derails the joint press conference by going off-script, solely blaming the late President Rayburn as the mastermind. Naturally, the room freezes, cameras roll, and suddenly, an international alliance teeters on the brink of collapse. Trowbridge's impulsive outburst is classic Diplomat chaos: equal parts political theater and raw emotion. He is the embodiment of a bruised ego, but one that's emblematic of Britain's frustration with being America's junior partner. Like most politicians, Trowbridge is determined to prove his dominance, even if it means destroying years of trust. The fallout is instant, leaving Kate scrambling to minimize the damage and Penn's administration in spin mode. 2 Grace Chooses Hal as Her Vice President Few moments this season sting quite like the reveal of Hal being tapped to become the next Vice President. It's a cruel twist that upends the entire dynamic of the central couple as Kate, who was long groomed for higher office, suddenly finds herself once again watching from the sidelines as her husband ascends to a role she could've taken. The decision may have been politically pragmatic, but it still cut right to the bone. Hal's new title also marks a new shift in their marriage. What was once settling into an equal partnership of shared ambition and intellect now becomes a source of resentment. And in true Diplomat fashion, the power shift doesn't just affect them personally — it tilts the entire show's moral balance. Specifically, Hal's ascent gives him proximity to President Penn — and with it, an outlet that enables him to willingly embrace the moral complexities of realpolitik. 1 The US Steals the Poseidon Keri Russell, Rufus Sewell. Allison Janney, Roy Kinnear, and David Gyasi in The Diplomat Season 3 finale. Image via Netflix There's no denying that Season 3's final reveal lands like a grenade . After spending a significant amount of time restoring diplomatic relationships, it all appears to crumble as Kate realizes the US orchestrated the unsanctioned removal of Russia's nuclear weapon, which also framed the UK in the process. Worse still, the operation was directed by her husband and President Penn, making the betrayal not only professional but personal. In many ways, the revelation reframes everything that came before. Every diplomatic crisis, every lie, every sacrifice suddenly looks like part of a much darker American agenda. So by the time Kate figures out the truth, she's staring down the potential collapse of her marriage, her career, and her faith in the institution she represents. It's a finale that doesn't just shock — it leaves you hollow, wondering if diplomacy itself can survive the very people sworn to uphold it. Oh, how emblematic of the real world this is. By Arielle Port Published 3 days ago Arielle Port started as a TV producer, developing content for Netflix (Firefly Lane, Brazen) and Hallmark (The Santa Stakeout, A Christmas Treasure) before transitioning into entertainment journalism. Her love of story went from interest to lifelong passion while at The University of Pennsylvania, where she fell in with a student-run web series, Classless TV, and it was a gateway drug. Arielle Port has been a Writer for Screen Rant since August 2024. She lives in Los Angeles with her boyfriend and more importantly, her cat, Boseman. Sign in to your ScreenRant account Summary Generate a summary of this story follow Follow followed Followed Like Like Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Sometimes the chemistry between two actors can be off, but never with these 10 TV couples, as they were either cast because they were already married or they fell in love in real life just like their characters do in the script. These TV relationships sparkle on screen, but they're even more meaningful to fans who know the backstory. Striking the right balance between not overplaying a will-they/won’t-they TV romance or boring audiences with a stable, happy relationship is a difficult task. These shows circumvented that problem by capitalizing on the natural chemistry between two actors who are married in real life, from supernatural romance to one of the best sitcom couples of all time . Angie D’Amato & Derek (Single Parents) Played By Spouses Leighton Meester & Adam Brody Leighton Meester and Adam Brody brought a gentle, unexpectedly tender spark to the underrated, short-lived sitcom Single Parents . Brody recurred as Derek, the long-absent father of Angie’s son, Graham. Though Derek is a minor character who only appears in season 2, their scenes have an unforced ease, the kind that can’t quite be manufactured. Angie is nudged toward Taran Killam’s character for Single Parent s’ central romantic arc, but whenever she and Derek share the screen, there’s a noticeable shift. The chemistry feels lived-in, a reminder of the real-life happiness Meester and Brody bring to their on-screen dynamic. This is a must-watch for anyone who wanted to see more of Meester in the cast of Nobody Wants This season 2 . Meester and Brody married in 2014, after filming The Oranges together in 2010. They have two children, daughter Arlo, born in 2015 and a son whose name has not been shared publicly, born in 2020. Sookie Stackhouse & Bill Compton (True Blood) Played By Future Spouses Anna Paquin & Stephen Moyer Sookie Stackhouse and Bill Compton talking in True Blood. When Anna Paquin and Stephen Moyer first met on the set of True Blood , they reportedly felt an instant spark. Their first screen test revealed a chemistry so natural it practically defined the tone for Sookie Stackhouse and Bill Compton’s turbulent yet passionate romance in True Blood — a relationship that became the emotional backbone of the show. As their characters navigated danger, longing, and supernatural drama, the real-life bond between Paquin and Moyer added an extra layer of authenticity. They eventually married in 2010 and went on to have two children in 2012, fraternal twins Charlie and Poppy, making their on- and off-screen partnership a true example of co-stars turned family. Elizabeth & Philip Jennings (The Americans) Played By Future Partners Keri Russell & Matthew Rhys Philip and Elizabeth in The Americans FX's excellent period spy drama The Americans may have centered on a fake marriage built on secrets, but it sparked a real and lasting partnership between Keri Russell and Matthew Rhys. The pair, who played undercover Soviet spies Elizabeth and Philip Jennings, developed their off-screen connection while filming the series and have been together since 2014. Though they casually refer to each other as husband and wife, they’ve admitted they haven’t actually gotten around to legally marrying — a detail that feels fittingly low-stress for a couple whose on-screen lives were anything but. They have a son, who was born in 2016, and their real relationship is free of the turmoil that defined their characters’ complex “ marriage of convenience .” Michael Kelso & Jackie Burkhart ('70s Show) Played By Future Spouses Ashton Kutcher & Mila Kunis That 70s Show Kelso and Jackie looking at each other Ashton Kutcher and Mila Kunis first met as teens on the set of That '70s Show , where they played the volatile, mismatched couple Michael Kelso and Jackie Burkhart. Kelso and Jackie were a comedic tornado — dramatic, shallow, and constantly breaking up — yet always drawn back to each other, a sharp contrast to Donna and Eric’s steadier, more grounded romance. Off-screen, Kutcher and Kunis didn’t date at the time, but years after the show ended, they reconnected and eventually married in 2015. Now parents to a daughter and a son, born in 2014 and 2016 respectively, they seem to share a unified rhythm in real life — something their fictional counterparts never managed, making the actors' love story a sweeter, more grounded echo of their sitcom beginnings. However rocky their relationship was as teens, Kelso and Jackie appear as a married couple in the spin-off series That '90s Show , a fun wink to fans who know the history of the actors. Ron Swanson & Tammy II (Parks & Recreation) Played By Spouses Nick Offerman & Megan Mullally Ron Swanson and Tammy II in Parks and Recreation are one of the sitcom's most chaotic delights — a toxic, explosive pairing whose sexual chemistry is pushed to gleeful, unhinged extremes. Every time they’re on-screen together, destruction follows, which makes it even funnier that they’re played by real-life spouses Nick Offerman and Megan Mullally. Offerman and Mullally, married since 2003, couldn’t be further from their characters’ combustible dynamic; their real life is famously calm and cozy, filled with jigsaw puzzles. Mullally once hosted Offerman as a guest on Will & Grace , and he returned the favor years later when she joined Parks & Rec as Ron’s terrifying ex-wife. Their gentle, funny dynamic shines on their podcast In Bed with Nick and Megan , where they share insights into their life together and interview guests. Charles Nieuwendyk & Mona Margadoff (A Man On The Inside) Played By Spouses Ted Danson & Mary Steenburgen Mary Steenburgen’s appearance in the cast of A Man on the Inside season 2 is incredibly charming, as it pairs her once again with her real-life husband, Ted Danson. Steenburgen, long considered the sunnier, more free-spirited half of their partnership, brings that same warmth to Mona Margadoff, a music professor who instantly captivates Danson’s tightly wound architecture professor, Charles Nieuwendyk. Their on-screen dynamic mirrors the balance they’ve shared for decades: his earnest precision softened by her effortless ease. Danson and Steenburgen have been married since 1995, a year after playing a married couple in Pontiac Moon . They also portrayed fictionalized versions of themselves in Curb Your Enthusiasm , with their characters hilariously getting divorced. Watching Danson express Charles’s attraction to Mona feels like a gentle echo of their real bond. It’s a delightful reminder of how much joy they still take in each other after so many decades. Though they have no children together, Danson and Steenburgen each have two children from previous marriages. Jon Snow & Ygritte (Game Of Thrones) Played By Future Spouses Kit Harington & Rose Leslie Kit Harington and Rose Leslie met on the set of Game of Thrones , where they played the star-crossed lovers Jon Snow and Ygritte. On screen, Jon and Ygritte’s romance was intense, fraught with danger, and ultimately tragic. It does not necessarily reflect the view of The Herald. The Beast in Me Netflix *** It was tucked away in STV’s late-night schedules, as if on a secret mission of its own. But for those who stumbled across it, The Americans was a prize find. Starring Keri Russell and Matthew Rhys as undercover KGB agents in suburban Washington, it ran for six award-winning series and did for spy dramas what Russell’s The Diplomat would later do for transatlantic political capers. Running during much of the same period was the equally mighty Homeland, starring Clare Danes as a CIA officer grappling with bipolar disorder and carrying the weight of the world on her shoulders (or so it seemed). Someone clever had the idea to pair Danes and Rhys, and the result is The Beast in Me — a high-octane psychological thriller streaming on Netflix from today. Rhys plays Nile Jarvis, a controversial New York property developer (is there any other kind?), whose wife has vanished under suspicious circumstances. Seeking time out of the media spotlight, Nile moves to deepest suburbia, where one of his neighbours is a reclusive author, Aggie Wiggs (Danes). Aggie is nursing a terrible loss of her own and a serious case of writer’s block. Initially, she wants nothing to do with her obscenely wealthy neighbour, his scary guard dogs, and his plans for a fancy jogging path through the woods. But needs must when you haven’t published anything in years and your old house is falling apart. So when Niles suggests himself as the subject of her next biography, Aggie is tempted. As you might expect, Danes and Rhys are wonderful together. Aggie is appalled by Niles, yet part of her admires his fearlessness and his determination to strike back at his enemies. She is angry at the world and what life has taken from her. Though still wary of her neighbour, like recognises like, and a strange fellowship begins. Head to Shetland Celebrity Traitors: As winner revealed, we’ve found perfect candidate for next series Scottish medical student lifts one of TV's biggest trophies The premise is intriguing — In Cold Blood meets Succession meets What Lies Beneath. For most of the eight episodes, The Beast in Me is irresistibly binge-worthy. Behind the camera, the classy cast is matched by Jodie Foster and Homeland creator Howard Gordon as producers. If you can get over a jump-the-shark moment partway through, the story just about gets back on track by the end. More of a problem is the violence. You never see the blows land directly, but the other sights and sounds are disturbing enough. While Danes is on the whole terrific, her character goes from 0 to 11 on the overwrought scale and stays there for eight episodes. Aggie is not quite as intense as Homeland’s Carrie. Even so, it is a close-run thing and often exhausting to watch. By way of distractions, there are subplots involving a power-hungry local politician and an FBI agent obsessed with bringing Niles down. Rhys is excellent as the stylish sociopath and spoiled little rich kid, all charm one minute, full of menace the next. They should have him guest-star in The Diplomat.
