text: The secrets of Britain’s costume king — and how he dresses the stars , The Sunday Times Today's Quizle Q: Test your knowledge Y ou might not recognise the name, but you’ll certainly recognise John Bright’s work. Tiny, softly spoken and with an impish grin, the 85-year-old is behind some of the most beautiful costumes in film — from Meryl Streep’s silk wedding skirt suit and hat in Out of Africa to Helena Bonham Carter’s dresses in A Room with a View . His company, Cosprop, based in an unassuming office building on Holloway Road in north London, has been the driving force behind Britain’s thriving costume industry for 60 years. Its success is emblematic of the prestige of Britain’s entire costume industry. The costumes made here have had a pivotal role in putting British films and television shows on the map — and in attracting directors from around the world to make their productions here. Last year the British and Irish box office totalled £979 million, and £5.6 billion was spent on film and TV production in the UK. When I speak to Adrian Wootton, the chief executive of Film London and the British Film Commission, he tells me that costume makes a significant contribution to these figures. “Britain punches massively above its weight when it comes to film,” and that is in large part down to “the incredible tradition of craftsmanship in the UK”. Costume, he says, “is one of the reasons why we are so attractive to international and US productions. They can draw on all those incredible skills and they know they won’t have to bring lots of people with them because we’ve got them all here.” Helena Bonham Carter as Lucy Honeychurch in A Room with a View (1985) ALAMY Inside Cosprop, the staff are busy working on costumes for the forthcoming Harry Potter series. There are skills on show that you cannot quite believe still exist. In the dye room an enormous cauldron bubbles dark pink. In alterations industrial irons spit out steam. And when I visited 85 mannequins lined a corridor, ready to be dressed for the Fashion & Textile Museum’s exhibition Costume Couture: Sixty Years of Cosprop . They will be transformed into some of the most recognisable characters in British cinema, including Onegin ’s red-gowned Tatyana Larina, as played by Liv Tyler, and Emma Thompson’s demure Elinor Dashwood from Sense & Sensibility . Advertisement The exhibition is a landmark moment for the company, but it also raises questions about the future of costume. Despite their global reputation, costume houses have faced threat after threat over the past five years: Covid, which made fittings impossible and put commissioning on hold; the financial devastation caused by the Hollywood writers’ strikes — Cosprop lost £750,000 during that time — and now the looming possibility of AI and special effects replacing their craft. Can Britain retain its costume crown for another 60 years? • Costume Couture review — a wander through cinema’s best wardrobe Where once Cosprop would have been asked to provide every single costume for a production, now it might only dress the principal actors — with the rest designed in-house. Cosprop’s manager Chris Garlick tells me that when it recently gave a quote for a Jane Austen production, which he delicately leaves unnamed, the producer asked if the company would do it for half the price. This tendency for thrift has been noticed by actors. “I do feel these things are being eroded because of budget concerns,” says the actor Toby Stephens, who is also keen to talk to me about Cosprop. Suited and booted: Meryl Streep in Out of Africa; Maggie Smith in Downton Abbey; Johnny Depp in Pirates of the Caribbean: On Stranger Tides CARNIVAL FILMS/GLOBE PHOTOS/ALAMY I sit down with Bright and he tells me that costume wasn’t his first love. “I always wanted to act, but my father wouldn’t allow it. He thought it was a sort of ragamuffin’s trade.” After taking a dress design course at South West Essex Technical College, followed by several hectic years building his skills in repertory theatre (earning “seven quid a week”), Bright decided to set up his own costume house in 1965. The timing was ideal, as the competition was beginning to struggle. Advertisement “A lot of the old costume houses were running out of steam and closing down. The main reason for that, I suppose, was colour television.” The bright, contrasting clothes that had worked in black-and-white looked terrible in colour, which required a more subtle touch. Bright, however, could build up stock suited to the new multicoloured world. John Bright, Cosprop’s founder VICKI COUCHMAN FOR THE SUNDAY TIMES He decided to use vintage fabrics where possible and make clothes to authentic patterns. As the actor Ralph Fiennes explains to me when we speak later, this authenticity gave Cosprop the edge. “Behind [Bright] are these incredible artefacts. Even if they are too precious to be worn, they are references for certain clothes being made.” Bright’s big break came when he was hired to make the costumes for the films of Ismail Merchant and James Ivory, which he worked on with the designer Jenny Beavan. The pair’s research methods were initially rather limited: for instance, for 1985’s A Room with a View they were given travel brochures of Florence and photographs by Fratelli Alinari as inspiration. But it was enough, Bright explains. These photos influenced the “black-and-white look of the Italians”, while the English characters were “a bit wishy-washy in colour”. • Merchant Ivory review — screen titans and secret lovers For many viewers, the most memorable scene in that film was when the costumes came off, and Julian Sands and Rupert Graves splashed around nude in a pond with Simon Callow — until they were interrupted by a horrified Helena Bonham Carter and Daniel Day-Lewis, clad all in white. “I wanted them to be as white as possible, to look like avenging angels,” Bright says with a chuckle. Advertisement Beavan, who was nine months pregnant at the time, has quite different memories of the scene. “We weren’t supposed to show their bits, because we knew [the film] was going to be shown to the Queen Mother, who obviously couldn’t have cared less, but you saw far more because [the pond] wasn’t as deep as it should have been,” she says. “I was racing around desperately trying to keep these hapless actors warm and dry.” Technical hitches aside, and with the Queen Mother’s approval, A Room with a View won the first of Cosprop’s 17 Oscars for costume design and its future was secured. And where Bright’s old-fashioned shyness might prevent him from waxing lyrical about his biggest hits — Merchant Ivory, Austen adaptations, great Russian productions — the actors who work with him are more than willing to do it for him. When I descended into Imelda Staunton’s dressing room at the Garrick Theatre, in London, where she was playing the lead in Mrs Warren’s Profession , her costumes for the play, all designed by Bright, were lined up on a rail. She showed me details on the dresses — a lace trim here, a brooch there — which were added by him. Jenna Coleman in Victoria; Alan Rickman in Sense and Sensibility; Helen Helen McCrory in Peaky Blinders GARETH GATRELL/ITV/ALAMY For Stephens, his first visit to Cosprop was a continuation of a family tradition. He tells me: “I remember going there and thinking, this is why I wanted to be an actor.” His father, Robert Stephens, and his mother, Maggie Smith, were both Cosprop regulars. Smith was “difficult”, he admits. “She was firm about what she did and didn’t want to wear.” Bright agrees. “Maggie Smith wasn’t that keen on green,” he says, laughing, before adopting a haughty tone. “She would say, ‘Oh, darling, you’re not going to put me in that green blouse again.’” He soon found the source of her dislike of the colour — Smith had been dressed in green for a school play, and her mother’s only comment afterwards was: “Whatever possessed them to put you in green?” The confession moved him — it was an insight into the vulnerability of the fitting process, no matter how famous the actor. Beavan emphasises this too: “You’re a therapist, you’re a mother, you’re a coffee maker, you’re a soother.” Advertisement But the vulnerabilities aren’t only faced by the actors. Trends have changed and that has an impact on costumes. When I ask Stephens about new shows such as Bridgerton and The Gilded Age , which utilise fantasy versions of period costumes, all bright, shiny colours and elastic, he is hesitant. “Period drama, quite rightly, has been reinvented for this generation, but one hopes there will continue to be care about accuracy. It sounds fastidious, but it matters if you want to do it right.” • Darcy’s scene-stealing wet shirt sells for £25,000 John Glaser, who designed the costumes for Bridgerton , has said: “We were trying to be period but also have some fantasy, and have some fun with it.” He sourced the clothes not from Cosprop but from Angels, the oldest costume supplier in the world, established in 1840. Angels is seeking external investment for the first time in its history. It hopes to raise millions of pounds by selling a minority stake in the business. Despite Cosprop being an obvious competitor, Garlick shows no hint of schadenfreude at its difficulties. “If Angels went bust that would be a disaster for us,” he says. The industry, he believes, depends on a rich ecosystem. Nicole Kidman in The Portrait of a Lady (1996) ALAMY As AI is used more across industries, what will it mean for costumes? Wootton says: “I’m sceptical about the idea of it ‘taking over’, but as for assisting and enabling creatives to realise their vision in more sophisticated ways? I think AI can and will do that and certainly it’s already a very significant part of visual effects.” How will it actually work? On this Wootton is less certain, but he imagines “designers working with visual effects technology to make bits of costume that they won’t realise as real objects but will essentially be merged with the real costume”. Beavan appears unconcerned about AI. “I do seem to have kept working pretty much nonstop.” She does, however, note the number of people who tell her that they love the “chrysalis” dress in the 2021 film Cruella , for which she won the Oscar for costume design. “Everyone says that’s one of their favourites — it was actually visual effects.” Advertisement Perhaps more terrifying for Cosprop than Covid or writers’ strikes is the imminent departure of Bright. He seems to have considered this anniversary an appropriate moment for retirement — he is 85, after all. Staunton expresses no little dissatisfaction about the matter. “He’s still as sharp and keen as he ever was, so I don’t know why the bloody hell he’s retiring!” • Why Cruella is 2021’s most fashionable film Modest as ever, Bright focuses on his employees when I ask him about his legacy. “Most of the people in the company have been here for a little while. I think quite a lot’s rubbed off, enough for them to be making their own decisions.” I meet two interns in the workroom, training alongside seamstresses who have been there for decades. This dedication to training up the next generation is key, Wootton agrees. “The UK film and television industries have spent more money and effort on skills training than probably any other country in the world.” It’s quaint, in a way, this argument that Britain’s film industry will thrive not due to evolving technology or bigger budgets, but thanks to people working with a needle and thread, or an iron, or a saucepan of dye. But while Cosprop is clearly looking to the future, the ethos seems to be that the old ways are often the best. Clothes are checked out on paper forms, and there is no digital catalogue of the million objects inside the warehouse. Dresses are taken apart and stitched back together by hand; pencil sketches plaster the walls of the milliner’s office. Cosprop costumes are often designed to be unobtrusive — to look like clothes rather than costumes — so it’s easy for them to go unnoticed. But when you tune in to the new series of SAS: Rogue Heroes , or if you watch Florence and the Machine’s new music video, Everybody Scream , look again at what the performers are wearing. That silk tie or well-worn waistcoat or pearl necklace might be the final trace of the brilliant mind of John Bright. Bright, however, could build up stock suited to the new multicoloured world. John Bright, Cosprop’s founder VICKI COUCHMAN FOR THE SUNDAY TIMES He decided to use vintage fabrics where possible and make clothes to authentic patterns. As the actor Ralph Fiennes explains to me when we speak later, this authenticity gave Cosprop the edge. “Behind [Bright] are these incredible artefacts. Even if they are too precious to be worn, they are references for certain clothes being made. ” Bright’s big break came when he was hired to make the costumes for the films of Ismail Merchant and James Ivory, which he worked on with the designer Jenny Beavan. The pair’s research methods were initially rather limited: for instance, for 1985’s A Room with a View they were given travel brochures of Florence and photographs by Fratelli Alinari as inspiration. But it was enough, Bright explains. These photos influenced the “black-and-white look of the Italians”, while the English characters were “a bit wishy-washy in colour”. • Merchant Ivory review — screen titans and secret lovers For many viewers, the most memorable scene in that film was when the costumes came off, and Julian Sands and Rupert Graves splashed around nude in a pond with Simon Callow — until they were interrupted by a horrified Helena Bonham Carter and Daniel Day-Lewis, clad all in white. “I wanted them to be as white as possible, to look like avenging angels,” Bright says with a chuckle. Beavan, who was nine months pregnant at the time, has quite different memories of the scene. “We weren’t supposed to show their bits, because we knew [the film] was going to be shown to the Queen Mother, who obviously couldn’t have cared less, but you saw far more because [the pond] wasn’t as deep as it should have been,” she says. “I was racing around desperately trying to keep these hapless actors warm and dry. ” Technical hitches aside, and with the Queen Mother’s approval, A Room with a View won the first of Cosprop’s 17 Oscars for costume design and its future was secured. And where Bright’s old-fashioned shyness might prevent him from waxing lyrical about his biggest hits — Merchant Ivory, Austen adaptations, great Russian productions — the actors who work with him are more than willing to do it for him. When I descended into Imelda Staunton’s dressing room at the Garrick Theatre, in London, where she was playing the lead in Mrs Warren’s Profession , her costumes for the play, all designed by Bright, were lined up on a rail. She showed me details on the dresses — a lace trim here, a brooch there — which were added by him. Jenna Coleman in Victoria; Alan Rickman in Sense and Sensibility; Helen Helen McCrory in Peaky Blinders GARETH GATRELL/ITV/ALAMY For Stephens, his first visit to Cosprop was a continuation of a family tradition. He tells me: “I remember going there and thinking, this is why I wanted to be an actor. ” His father, Robert Stephens, and his mother, Maggie Smith, were both Cosprop regulars. Smith was “difficult”, he admits. “She was firm about what she did and didn’t want to wear. “Maggie Smith wasn’t that keen on green,” he says, laughing, before adopting a haughty tone. “She would say, ‘Oh, darling, you’re not going to put me in that green blouse again. ’” He soon found the source of her dislike of the colour — Smith had been dressed in green for a school play, and her mother’s only comment afterwards was: “Whatever possessed them to put you in green?” The confession moved him — it was an insight into the vulnerability of the fitting process, no matter how famous the actor. Beavan emphasises this too: “You’re a therapist, you’re a mother, you’re a coffee maker, you’re a soother. ” But the vulnerabilities aren’t only faced by the actors. Trends have changed and that has an impact on costumes. When I ask Stephens about new shows such as Bridgerton and The Gilded Age , which utilise fantasy versions of period costumes, all bright, shiny colours and elastic, he is hesitant. “Period drama, quite rightly, has been reinvented for this generation, but one hopes there will continue to be care about accuracy. It sounds fastidious, but it matters if you want to do it right. ” • Darcy’s scene-stealing wet shirt sells for £25,000 John Glaser, who designed the costumes for Bridgerton , has said: “We were trying to be period but also have some fantasy, and have some fun with it. ” He sourced the clothes not from Cosprop but from Angels, the oldest costume supplier in the world, established in 1840. Angels is seeking external investment for the first time in its history. It hopes to raise millions of pounds by selling a minority stake in the business. Despite Cosprop being an obvious competitor, Garlick shows no hint of schadenfreude at its difficulties. “If Angels went bust that would be a disaster for us,” he says. The industry, he believes, depends on a rich ecosystem. Nicole Kidman in The Portrait of a Lady (1996) ALAMY As AI is used more across industries, what will it mean for costumes? Wootton says: “I’m sceptical about the idea of it ‘taking over’, but as for assisting and enabling creatives to realise their vision in more sophisticated ways? I think AI can and will do that and certainly it’s already a very significant part of visual effects. ” How will it actually work? On this Wootton is less certain, but he imagines “designers working with visual effects technology to make bits of costume that they won’t realise as real objects but will essentially be merged with the real costume”. Beavan appears unconcerned about AI. “I do seem to have kept working pretty much nonstop. ” She does, however, note the number of people who tell her that they love the “chrysalis” dress in the 2021 film Cruella , for which she won the Oscar for costume design. “Everyone says that’s one of their favourites — it was actually visual effects. ” Perhaps more terrifying for Cosprop than Covid or writers’ strikes is the imminent departure of Bright. He seems to have considered this anniversary an appropriate moment for retirement — he is 85, after all. Staunton expresses no little dissatisfaction about the matter. “He’s still as sharp and keen as he ever was, so I don’t know why the bloody hell he’s retiring!” • Why Cruella is 2021’s most fashionable film Modest as ever, Bright focuses on his employees when I ask him about his legacy. “Most of the people in the company have been here for a little while. I think quite a lot’s rubbed off, enough for them to be making their own decisions. ” I meet two interns in the workroom, training alongside seamstresses who have been there for decades. This dedication to training up the next generation is key, Wootton agrees. “The UK film and television industries have spent more money and effort on skills training than probably any other country in the world. ” It’s quaint, in a way, this argument that Britain’s film industry will thrive not due to evolving technology or bigger budgets, but thanks to people working with a needle and thread, or an iron, or a saucepan of dye. But while Cosprop is clearly looking to the future, the ethos seems to be that the old ways are often the best. Clothes are checked out on paper forms, and there is no digital catalogue of the million objects inside the warehouse. Dresses are taken apart and stitched back together by hand; pencil sketches plaster the walls of the milliner’s office. Cosprop costumes are often designed to be unobtrusive — to look like clothes rather than costumes — so it’s easy for them to go unnoticed. But when you tune in to the new series of SAS: Rogue Heroes , or if you watch Florence and the Machine’s new music video, Everybody Scream , look again at what the performers are wearing. That silk tie or well-worn waistcoat or pearl necklace might be the final trace of the brilliant mind of John Bright. Katie Price's daughter makes prestigious Tatler list alongside fellow nepo babies and daughters of Dukes Tatler's Little Black Book features the list of eligible bachelorette's in the UK READ MORE: The 87 most eligible bachelors in Britain By ELMIRA TANATAROVA, ASSISTANT LIFESTYLE EDITOR and MONIQUE RUBINS, LIFESTYLE REPORTER and MARIA CHIORANDO, SENIOR REPORTER and ALICE WADE, LIFESTYLE REPORTER and POPPY ATKINSON GIBSON, LIFESTYLE REPORTER and ALANAH KHOSLA, SENIOR LIFESTYLE REPORTER and ELEANOR DYE, SENIOR LIFESTYLE REPORTER and JESSICA GREEN, ASSISTANT LIFESTYLE EDITOR Published: 20:22 EST, 12 November 2025 | Updated: 07:42 EST, 13 November 2025 e-mail 6 shares 288 View comments Tatler has unveiled its annual list of the most eligible young women in Britain and naturally it's awash with the daughters of Earls and Dukes, high society scions and sporting stars, actors and musicians. Perhaps the most surprising addition to the 2025 Little Black Book is descended from reality TV royalty rather than Kings and Queens - in the form of 18-year-old Princess Andre . The aspiring TV star and influencer, daughter of Katie Price and her ex-husband Peter, has won a coveted spot on the list of 112 bright young things under the age of 34 alongside a host of fellow nepo babies . She's joined by Lola Consuelos, daughter of US TV star Kelly Ripa , Nicole Kidman 's niece Lucia Hawley and Romy Curran whose mother is Bridget Jones author Helen Fielding. Others have been lauded on the list for their talent alone, including songbird Olivia Dean, 26, who has wowed critics with her soulful, feel-good hits such as Man I Need. Sports stars like tennis player Isabelle Lacy, 19, who made her Wimbledon debut in 2023, also made the cut. Socially media savvy has been rewarded too. Among the influencers is Tobi Ojora, who describes her content as 'facts, face, fitness, fashion’. Princess Andre Princess Andre (pictured) - the daughter of Katie Price and Peter Andre - was an unexpected addition in Tatler's top ten 'Best Dressed In Britain' stars this year, securing second place Princess Andre - the daughter of Katie Price and Peter Andre - made the list - and was also an unexpected addition in Tatler's top ten 'Best Dressed In Britain' stars this year, securing second place. The 18-year-old, who bagged herself an impressive deal with PrettyLittleThing last year, has enjoyed a meteoric rise to fame in recent years, and has been cashing in on brand deals as well as TV fame. She has already signed big money deals with clothing and beauty brands including Superdrug, Studio London, Morphe and Revolution. The model has amassed more than 743,000 followers on her Instagram and has vowed to become a 'millionaire by the age of 20'. In 2024, Princess also made her modelling debut with PrettyLittleThing after signing a four-figure deal with the brand. 'The daughter of glamour model Katie Price and 1990s pop heartthrob Peter Andre is the face of a new generation of British pop culture royalty,' the magazine stated. 'At just 18, the world is her oyster, and with her babydoll eyes, blonde beachy waves down to her hips and wardrobe of Y2K revival hits, this Princess is ready for her crown.' Lola Consuelos American singer-songwriter Lola Consuelos (pictured) is the daughter of US television personalities Kelly Ripa and Mark Consuelos American singer-songwriter Lola Consuelos is the daughter of US television personalities Kelly Ripa and Mark Consuelos. Raised in New York, the 24-year-old is now believed to be based predominantly in London following her graduation from the prestigious NYU. She debuted her first single, Paranoia Silverlining, in 2022, and has more upcoming releases, with a new EP, titled Sorry, It’s All About Me, which she will celebrate with a party in December. She has insisted she 'doesn't need to be in a relationship to survive' and admitted that she sees finding love as 'mystical' - as she's learned 'not to take any s*** from people'. Posing for a special digital shoot with ELLE UK , Olivia continued: 'It's this thing we all crave but aren't taught how to do it properly. Why don't we have a module at school? 'So, the album was just me zooming into that and looking at the last two years of my life and everything I've learned until now.' It even featured in British Vogue back in January, with Thyra writing at the time: 'So excited by this! Feeling very proud.' Thyra graduated this summer, after completing a study abroad programme at the Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona in Spain. She is also a passionate writer, frequently sharing articles on her Substack. Phoebe was the creative director of top design house Chloé between 2001 and 2006. During that time, one of her most famous creations - the Paddington bag - was first seen at Chloé's spring/summer 2005 show. The slouchy, boho creation - with its distinct leather covered oversized padlock detail - was coveted by all fashionistas. Now, in a neat cycle that fashion is known for, boho is firmly back - and one of the models who has worn the style on the catwalk is Maya. In fact, in March this year, Maya walked for Chloé - some 20 years after her mother had taken the helm at the brand, suggesting that at her tender age, she has adopted some impressive style credentials. Since then, Maya has appeared in Vogue France and Pop Magazine as well as top brands, including modelling for Gucci and closing Burberry's 2024 Autumn/Winter catwalk show. And the model, from West London, is also known to rub shoulders with other famous faces, including Romeo Beckham, when she's not globetrotting and sharing her Mediterranean adventures with her followers. Hunter’s Must-See Broadway Debut Reviews Review: Little Bear Ridge Road , Samuel D. Hunter’s Must-See Broadway Debut Laurie Metcalf and Micah Stock return to Broadway in a new play by Samuel D. Hunter. Zachary Stewart | Broadway | October 30, 2025 Laurie Metcalf and Micah Stock star in Samuel D. Hunter’s Little Bear Ridge Road , directed by Joe Mantello, at Broadway’s Booth Theatre. (© Julieta Cervantes) The couch is practically a fourth character in Samuel D. Hunter’s new drama Little Bear Ridge Road , which marks the acclaimed playwright’s Broadway debut. Upholstered in an ugly light tan leather, it’s the kind of sofa built for comfort rather than beauty, sporting a central foldout panel with cupholders and reclining functions on both ends. The only item of furniture on the circular platform at the center of Scott Pask’s simultaneously spare and cavernous set, it looks like the star attraction in a Raymour & Flanigan showroom, the cushy consolation prize for losing the American rat race. We first see Ethan (Micah Stock) and his aunt Sarah (Laurie Metcalf) standing in front of the couch—her couch. It’s 2020 and Ethan has returned from Seattle to Troy, Idaho to settle his recently deceased father’s estate, which sounds a lot grander than the $8,000 he will receive once he sells dad’s house and pays off his debt. Sarah knows Ethan doesn’t have money for a hotel and will probably sleep in his car rather than crash at the childhood home he now owns, the place where he suffered horrific abuse at the hands of his meth-addicted parent. She offers him her spare bedroom. In the limbo of the pandemic, weeks turn into months turn into years. Ethan has no desire to return to his old life as an unpublished writer and retail worker in Seattle. Nor does he see a clear path back out of Idaho. But he finds purpose in caring for Sarah, who is privately struggling with her health. Ethan is determined to help her, whether she wants it or not. Laurie Metcalf plays Sarah, and Micah Stock plays Ethan in Samuel D. Hunter’s Little Bear Ridge Road , directed by Joe Mantello, at Broadway’s Booth Theatre. (© Julieta Cervantes) Hunter’s play Grangeville , which made its world premiere earlier this year at Signature Theatre, was similarly powered by the tension between personal aspiration and family obligation, a specter that eventually haunts all Americans. In the grand sweep of history, we are odd ducks for regularly choosing personal fulfillment over filial piety. But what if your father is a dead drug addict? What if your dream career never panned out? And what if you face rejection even in your fallback position as a not particularly skilled trad nephew ? This is the awful fate Ethan shares with millions of Americans who have been relegated to the clearance shelf of the marketplace of human capital . Their voices are rarely heard on a Broadway stage, which makes Little Bear Ridge Road a tiny miracle of the fall season. We can feel Ethan’s percolating dread in every brilliant beat of Stock’s cringe-manufacturing performance. His eye-rolling deadpan is the unmistakable affectation of a gay man who has learned to feign casual disinterest as a defense mechanism. If he cannot find a purpose, maybe there is no purpose to anything. When he finally allows that emotional dam to break, it drowns the audience in a deluge of tears. Stock is a notably ugly crier. While he always sounds a little drunk, his diction is particularly fuzzy (without ever surrendering to incoherence) in the scene in which he first meets James (John Drea), a master’s student at the nearby University of Idaho. They meet at a bar for a Grindr date, and it’s clear that Ethan is expecting more grind than date. “I’m not gonna like, suck your dick at the Wagon Wheel,” James tells him, and Ethan’s disappointment is palpable. Yet both men stick around and form something resembling a relationship. Is it convenience or true love? Drea makes a convincing argument for the latter in a beautiful and emotionally unguarded performance. Late in the play, when James makes a breathtakingly vulnerable admission, Ethan responds by retreating into his phone. The inane drone of back-to-back Instagram reels has never sounded more devastating. Laurie Metcalf and Micah Stock star in Samuel D. Hunter’s Little Bear Ridge Road , directed by Joe Mantello, at Broadway’s Booth Theatre. (© Julieta Cervantes) “I’m tired of being your excuse, Ethan,” Sarah tells him in one of her more serious lines, which lands with the impact of a meteorite. Hunter has clearly tailored Sarah’s lines to Metcalf’s distinctive voice, and that bespoke treatment pays off throughout the play’s 90 minutes (it was a Steppenwolf commission, and brought Metcalf back to their Chicago stage last year for the first time in decades). Metcalf fracks humor from the dourest of circumstances, earning laughs through her singular portrayal of an older woman who is a bit set in her ways and would like to be left alone. Yet her kindness is unmistakable. It’s the strange combination of care and emotional detachment that one frequently finds in a longtime nurse like Sarah. Director Joe Mantello wisely understands that he need not do much to garnish such tremendously rich performances, which are the main attraction of Little Bear Ridge Road . Jessica Pabst’s costumes convey affordable comfort (Metcalf is wearing the exact socks my sister once bought me for a Christmas stocking-stuffer). Sound designer Mikhail Fiksel walks the border between banality and magic, creating little noises from the prestige television dramas that our characters, seated on the couch , consume while eating from little ceramic bowls—bread and circuses for the age of social atomization. Heather Gilbert’s subtly suggestive lighting brings us out of Sarah’s living room and occasionally astounds us with the adamantine enormity of Pask’s upstage wall, which suggests a world that will endure beyond our brief and transient lives. But those fleeting moments are where we live, and they deserve attention and care. Little Bear Ridge Road is a quietly triumphant debut for Hunter, an American playwright who sees the country we truly inhabit, rather than the one we like to imagine we do. Videos 2025 Movie Releases Screenings What to Watch Originals Reviews Close ‘Scream 7’ Star Teases “Genius” Return to Franchise For Original 'Scream' Writer and Neve Campbell [Exclusive] SCREAM 4, (aka SCRE4M), Neve Campbell, 2011 Image via Phil Bray/©Dimension Films/courtesy Everett Collection By Britta DeVore & Perri Nemiroff Published Nov 4, 2025 Sign in to your Collider account Summary Generate a summary of this story follow Follow followed Followed Like Like Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap At this point in his career, Asa Germann is best known for busting through walls like the Kool-Aid Man and leaning into a redemption arc as Sam Riordan on Prime Video’s hit series, Gen V , but that’s all about to change. The actor, who also enjoyed a brief appearance on the first season of Netflix’s smash-hit anthology project, Monster , will soon appear on the big screen in a new installment of one of the most beloved horror franchises of all time. On February 27, Germann will join a stacked call sheet of newcomers and familiar faces alike when he appears in Scream 7 . As we creep closer to the release of the first in-series movie to be helmed by universe creator, Kevin Williamson , audiences are itching with anticipation to see what kinds of tricks and treats are in store. And, although no trailer has been dropped at this time, Perri Nemiroff got the next best thing — a few comments from Germann about his attachment to the film during a recent installment of Collider Forces following the Gen V Season 2 finale. Germann is just like those of us at home, who look to the Scream franchise as our warm blanket and comfort movies during troubled times, telling Nemiroff, “First of all, I'm a huge, huge fan of any kind of iconic cinema like that. Scream is a massive, massive thing , as you know, and really redefined the horror genre , and kind of set the tone for the next decade of not only film but TV, too.” Teasing how hard the Williamson-directed production will swing, he added, “I would say, in retrospect, the thing that was most exciting to me about doing Scream was Kevin Williamson. This is the first one that Kevin's directed. Kevin, who created Scream and Dawson's Creek and Vampire Diaries and Cruel Intentions, and so many things, who is the greatest guy. Getting to be a part of his journey in such a significant way was so cool. Getting to be a part of that ensemble, with all those people that have been involved in the film for so long… And I'm not going to say in what capacity… But nonetheless, stepping into that was one of the coolest things ever. I think people are going to love it. I think people are going to be really, really impressed with Kevin's foray into directing Scream . He's a genius. ” Of the killer ensemble driving the movie’s plot, which will reintroduce Neve Campbell ’s Sidney Prescott as the main character after taking a backseat in 2022’s Scream and removing herself from the equation in 2023’s Scream VI , Germann said he was most blown away sharing the set with the movie series’ two final girls — Campbell and Courteney Cox . Referring to the awe-inspiring moments of working alongside the two powerhouses, the Gen V star said, “I mean, Courteney [Cox] is crazy because Friends is amazing. Then Neve [Campbell] is one of the coolest people alive.” Although this may have been the first time his paths crossed with the legacy actresses, it was a reunion for him and several friends, he added, “ Mason Gooding is someone that I knew previously who is a good buddy of mine, and same with Jasmin [ Savoy Brown ], and Sam Rechner , who's a new guy, and Isabel May . The list goes on and on. Celeste O'Connor , Joel McHale .” A Shoutout to the Greats of the Scream Franchise Neve Campbell as Sidney Prescott and Laurie Metcalf as Mrs. Loomis in Scream 2. With the plot under lock and key , Germann understandably couldn’t tease anything about his character, but his nod to the Ghostfaces that came before might allude to his allegiances. Then again, he might just be pointing out a handful of the horror world’s greatest performances of all time. “If I could go back and give someone a shout-out from the Scream franchise that I think doesn’t get enough attention, I would give Laurie Metcalf … Round of applause for Laurie Metcalf… Scream 2 is one of the best Screams , by the way… Also, Dermot Mulroney . We gotta give a shout-out to Dermot Mulroney… He's having fun. I've known Dermot my whole life, and I've always been such a huge fan of him. He's such a great actor.” And, when asked which character he’d happily take over from a previous movie if given the chance, Germann was clear that Matthew Lillard ’s Stu Macher is a dream role — which we could totally see. Noting that the character’s scenes at “the end of the first one” are standout, Germann continued, “When he says, ‘My mom and dad are gonna be so mad at me!’ I know he improvised that line, too, which is hysterical. I love Matthew Lillard. As an actor, I've always been a fan of his, from like SLC Punk! and Wicker Park , which is a movie that I don't know if people have even seen.” Stay tuned to Collider for more about Scream 7 and head over to Prime Video to stream Seasons 1 and 2 of Gen V in their entirety. Videos 2025 Movie Releases Screenings What to Watch Originals Reviews Close ‘Scream 7’ Star Teases “Genius” Return to Franchise For Original 'Scream' Writer and Neve Campbell [Exclusive] SCREAM 4, (aka SCRE4M), Neve Campbell, 2011 Image via Phil Bray/©Dimension Films/courtesy Everett Collection By Britta DeVore & Perri Nemiroff Published Nov 4, 2025 Sign in to your Collider account Summary Generate a summary of this story follow Follow followed Followed Like Like Thread Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap At this point in his career, Asa Germann is best known for busting through walls like the Kool-Aid Man and leaning into a redemption arc as Sam Riordan on Prime Video’s hit series, Gen V , but that’s all about to change. The actor, who also enjoyed a brief appearance on the first season of Netflix’s smash-hit anthology project, Monster , will soon appear on the big screen in a new installment of one of the most beloved horror franchises of all time. On February 27, Germann will join a stacked call sheet of newcomers and familiar faces alike when he appears in Scream 7. As we creep closer to the release of the first in-series movie to be helmed by universe creator, Kevin Williamson , audiences are itching with anticipation to see what kinds of tricks and treats are in store. And, although no trailer has been dropped at this time, Perri Nemiroff got the next best thing — a few comments from Germann about his attachment to the film during a recent installment of Collider Forces following the Gen V Season 2 finale. Germann is just like those of us at home, who look to the Scream franchise as our warm blanket and comfort movies during troubled times, telling Nemiroff, “First of all, I'm a huge, huge fan of any kind of iconic cinema like that. Scream is a massive, massive thing , as you know, and really redefined the horror genre , and kind of set the tone for the next decade of not only film but TV, too. ” Teasing how hard the Williamson-directed production will swing, he added, “I would say, in retrospect, the thing that was most exciting to me about doing Scream was Kevin Williamson. This is the first one that Kevin's directed. Kevin, who created Scream and Dawson's Creek and Vampire Diaries and Cruel Intentions, and so many things, who is the greatest guy. Getting to be a part of his journey in such a significant way was so cool. Getting to be a part of that ensemble, with all those people that have been involved in the film for so long… And I'm not going to say in what capacity… But nonetheless, stepping into that was one of the coolest things ever. I think people are going to love it. I think people are going to be really, really impressed with Kevin's foray into directing Scream. ” Of the killer ensemble driving the movie’s plot, which will reintroduce Neve Campbell ’s Sidney Prescott as the main character after taking a backseat in 2022’s Scream and removing herself from the equation in 2023’s Scream VI , Germann said he was most blown away sharing the set with the movie series’ two final girls — Campbell and Courteney Cox. Referring to the awe-inspiring moments of working alongside the two powerhouses, the Gen V star said, “I mean, Courteney [Cox] is crazy because Friends is amazing. Then Neve [Campbell] is one of the coolest people alive. ” Although this may have been the first time his paths crossed with the legacy actresses, it was a reunion for him and several friends, he added, “ Mason Gooding is someone that I knew previously who is a good buddy of mine, and same with Jasmin [ Savoy Brown ], and Sam Rechner , who's a new guy, and Isabel May. The list goes on and on. Celeste O'Connor , Joel McHale. ” A Shoutout to the Greats of the Scream Franchise Neve Campbell as Sidney Prescott and Laurie Metcalf as Mrs. With the plot under lock and key , Germann understandably couldn’t tease anything about his character, but his nod to the Ghostfaces that came before might allude to his allegiances. Then again, he might just be pointing out a handful of the horror world’s greatest performances of all time. “If I could go back and give someone a shout-out from the Scream franchise that I think doesn’t get enough attention, I would give Laurie Metcalf … Round of applause for Laurie Metcalf… Scream 2 is one of the best Screams , by the way… Also, Dermot Mulroney. We gotta give a shout-out to Dermot Mulroney… He's having fun. I've known Dermot my whole life, and I've always been such a huge fan of him. He's such a great actor. ” And, when asked which character he’d happily take over from a previous movie if given the chance, Germann was clear that Matthew Lillard ’s Stu Macher is a dream role — which we could totally see. Noting that the character’s scenes at “the end of the first one” are standout, Germann continued, “When he says, ‘My mom and dad are gonna be so mad at me!’ I know he improvised that line, too, which is hysterical. As an actor, I've always been a fan of his, from like SLC Punk! and Wicker Park , which is a movie that I don't know if people have even seen. ” Stay tuned to Collider for more about Scream 7 and head over to Prime Video to stream Seasons 1 and 2 of Gen V in their entirety. Courtesy of Jodi Gardi By Staten Island Community News STATEN ISLAND, NY — Sea View Playwright’s Theatre will open Edward Albee’s Pulitzer Prize-winning play “Three Tall Women” today for a two-weekend run at its Staten Island location. The production features Regina Paleau as “A”, Cheryl Grogan-Wagner as “B,” and Emma White as “C,” under the direction of Craig Stoebling. The show will run for five performances through Nov. 23. Albee’s play tells the story of three women in two distinct parts. The first half presents a naturalistic conversation between a wealthy nonagenarian known as “A,” her middle-aged caretaker “B,” and a young lawyer “C.” In the second half, the three women transform into personifications of the same woman at different ages — 92, 52, and 26 — as they confront her life, memories and regrets. The play is largely autobiographical and based on Albee’s contentious relationship with his adopted mother. It explores themes of aging, memory, and self-deception through the interactions of the three characters. “Three Tall Women” premiered off-Broadway in 1994 and won the Pulitzer Prize for Drama that year. The play made its London West End debut in 1995, featuring Maggie Smith in the role of “A,” and returned to Broadway in 2018 with Glenda Jackson as “A” and Laurie Metcalf as “B,” winning the Tony Award for Best Revival of a Play. Albee has long been considered one of America’s foremost playwrights. His works include “The Zoo Story,” “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” and “The Goat, or Who Is Sylvia?” In 2023, Sea View Playwright’s Theatre produced Albee’s “Who’s Afraid of Virginia Woolf?” and “At Home at the Zoo,” which were partially funded by a NYSCA grant through Staten Island Arts. Performances of “Three Tall Women” are scheduled for today, Saturday, Nov. 15, at 8 p.m.; Sunday, Nov. 16, at 2 p.m.; Friday, Nov. 21, at 8 p.m., Saturday, Nov. 22, at 8 p.m., and Sunday, Nov. 23, at 2 p.m. The theater is located at 460 Brielle Ave., Sea View. Tickets: $42- $56 (discounts available) Mosaictheater.org With each new work, Samuel D. Hunter has become more interested in “big ideas thriving in small containers.” Increasingly, he likes to write plays with very few characters and simple sets. His 2022 two-person play, “A Case for the Existence of God,” (now running at Mosaic Theater Company) is one of these minimal pieces. “Audiences might come in expecting a theological debate set in the Vatican, but instead it’s two guys sitting in a cubicle discussing terms on a bank loan,” says Hunter (who goes by Sam). Like many of his plays, this award-winning work unfolds in rural Idaho, where Hunter was raised. Two men, one gay, the other straight (here played by local out actors Jaysen Wright and Lee Osorio, respectively), bond over financial insecurity and the joys and challenges of single fatherhood. His newest success is similarly reduced. Touted as Hunter’s long-awaited Broadway debut, “Little Bear Ridge Road” features Laurie Metcalf as Sarah and Micah Stock as Ethan, Sarah’s estranged gay nephew who returns to Idaho from Seattle to settle his late father’s estate. Tickets starting at $67 Broadwayatthenational.com For more than a year, out actor Edward Juvier has been part of the national tour of “Some Like It Hot,” the musical adaption of the 1959 classic comedy starring Marilyn Monroe and written and directed by Billy Wilder. Juvier, 49, plays Osgood Fielding III, a cheery millionaire in Depression-era America. With music by Marc Shaiman, lyrics by Scott Wittman and Shaiman, and a book by Matthew López and Amber Ruffin, the 2022 musical is quite different as well with diverse casting, increasingly complicated backstories, and a non-binary character (Daphne). A talented tenor and Houston native, Juvier is a Cuban American who’s been working in musical theater since graduating from the Boston Conservatory in 2000. “I personally love touring,” says Juvier. “I like the life on the road and visiting these old theater houses across the country. Seeing the locals that I remember and my friends and family that live all over. For me, a transient life is great. Maybe not so great for others.” Early in his career, he toured with “Phantom of the Opera” for six years. He began in the ensemble and covered two principal roles, and moved to swing which gave him the longevity covering 11 different roles in that show, a life-changing gig that he remembers fondly. WASHINGTON BLADE: As a gay actor touring in a hot musical with some queer themes do you feel that you make an impact? EDWARD JUVIER: Oh yeah, it’s important for queer people to see representation on stage. Our version of the show is a sneak attack; it doesn’t hit you over the head with themes. Seeing an old story that takes a turn where you’re left to accept what’s happening onstage and by that time, you’re in love and rooting with the characters. You feel it from the audiences and we play some of the reddest of states. Queer, trans, nonbinary people meet us at the stage door in tears thanking us for the representation. They didn’t even know when they came to the show that they’re going to see something with such an affirming message to their lives, and they’re thrilled when they find that out. BLADE: How were you drawn into musical theater? JUVIER: I was lucky that my Texas high school made annual trips to New York to see Broadway shows. On one trip, I remember seeing “Will Rogers Follies,” I felt like Keith Carradine was looking and talking right to me. And the next day, we saw “Falsettos,” the original production. After seeing those two very different shows it was as if I blasted off into the Broadway world. BLADE: Did “Falsettos,” a musical about AIDS, resonate with you as young gay student? JUVIER: Absolutely. It shook me to the core. BLADE: Has being gay made you a better actor? JUVIER: I think what makes a great actor is somebody who has enormous empathy, able to put themselves in someone else’s shoes, and what better than a queer artist to be able to empathize. Continue Reading Theater Astounding ‘LIZZIE’ builds on legendary axe murder tale Rock musical twist addresses abuse, oppression, queer identity Published 3 weeks ago on November 9, 2025 By Patrick Folliard Caroline Graham and Sydne Lyons play the Borden sisters in ‘LIZZIE.’ (Photo by Cameron Whitman) ‘LIZZIE’ Through Nov. 30 Keegan Theatre 1742 Church St., N.W. $54-$65 Keegantheatre.com Lizzie Borden put Fall River, Mass., on the map. When the 32-year-old, seemingly respectable woman was charged with the axe murder of her father Andrew and stepmother Abby in the summer of 1892, it sent shock waves across the community and far beyond. In time, the gruesome tale would weave its way into the annals of American crime lore, always remembered through that popular nursery rhyme “Lizzie Borden took an axe, gave her father 40 whacks…” Well, you know the rest. The astoundingly terrific “LIZZIE” (now playing at Keegan Theatre, a short walk from Dupont Circle Metro) builds on the legend. The rock musical with book by Tim Maner, music by Steven Cheslik-deMeyer and Alan Stevens Hewitt, and lyrics by Cheslik-deMeyer and Maner, follows the days leading up to the grisly murders (unseen offstage) through Lizzie’s acquittal, bringing to the fore matters of abuse, oppression, and queer identity. Shrewdly staged and choreographed by Jennifer J. Hopkins, the show begins with a haunting version of “Forty Whacks (Prologue),” featuring the talented cast of four women who can sing, act, move, and deliver the occasional laugh-out-loud line. Clearly, frustrated Lizzie (powerfully played by Caroline Graham) and dominant older sister Emma (Sydne Lyon), both unmarried and still at home, are angsty and deeply unhappy. They resent their father for a litany of reasons including his extreme Yankee frugality. While one of the richest men in Fall River, he chooses to live on a sad street and go without indoor plumbing rather than set up housekeeping in posh digs across town. But it’s when they see Andrew’s great fortune slipping away to their stepmother that their fury reaches new heights. Much of “LIZZIE” takes place at the scene of the crime, the Borden residence – cleverly suggested by scenic designer Josh Sticklin with some clapboard siding, stairways, a bit of period wallpaper and a purposely incongruous, large Borden family coat of arms. Lighting designer Sage Green, convincingly and evocatively, summons at turns a bona fide rock concert experience, dimly lit parlor, or an intimate setting in a small yard. And costume designer Logan Benson savvily adds to the atmosphere. Lizzie’s somber dresses with their accurate to the era leg-of-mutton sleeves give way to something altogether glitzier and more revealing after the murders. There is dialogue, but the Riot Grrrl-inspired work is mostly sung through with punk rock anthems, ballads, and character driven songs. Whether spoken or sung, “LIZZIE” makes no bones about the title character’s guilt while introducing varying levels of collusion among the other women. A knowing wry smirk from the house maid Bridget (Brigid Wallace Harper) says a lot about the family dynamic (“there’s a lock on every door / In every room a prisoner of a long, silent war”) as well as what went down that summer morning at the Borden house. Lizzie’s secret girlfriend Alice (golden throated Savannah Blackwell) who conveniently lives next door, is besotted and watches her every move. Just after the murders, she saw Lizzie burn a dress in the yard. The hard driving score is played by a passionate half-dozen strong band led by Marika Countouris. Sometimes, the instruments overpower the amplified singers and a lyric or two is lost, but that’s not so unusual with rock musicals. At 90 minutes with a leisurely intermission (well-earned by the band and cast, especially Graham as Lizzie who’s onstage throughout, often incorporating frenetic movement and strenuous air guitar into her many songs), the first half explores feelings of entrapment and the second liberation. Lizzie goes to trial. Despite a shaky alibi, the defendant seems to be winning over the jury. Looks like she might get that grand house on the hill after all. The Borden story has been shared in varied ways including innumerable books and documentaries, Jack Beeson’s opera “Lizzie Borden” (1965), Agnes de Mille’s ballet “Fall River Legend” (1954), and the memorable 1975 TV movie starring Elizabeth Montgomery (best known as the perky reluctant witch Samantha Stevens on TV’s sitcom “Bewitched”) playing against type. Today, the legend endures with “LIZZIE” at Keegan. (Photo by Matthew Murphy) ‘Some Like It Hot’ Nov. 7 The National Theatre 1321 Pennsylvania Ave. Tickets starting at $67 Broadwayatthenational. com For more than a year, out actor Edward Juvier has been part of the national tour of “Some Like It Hot,” the musical adaption of the 1959 classic comedy starring Marilyn Monroe and written and directed by Billy Wilder. Juvier, 49, plays Osgood Fielding III, a cheery millionaire in Depression-era America. With music by Marc Shaiman, lyrics by Scott Wittman and Shaiman, and a book by Matthew López and Amber Ruffin, the 2022 musical is quite different as well with diverse casting, increasingly complicated backstories, and a non-binary character (Daphne). A talented tenor and Houston native, Juvier is a Cuban American who’s been working in musical theater since graduating from the Boston Conservatory in 2000. “I personally love touring,” says Juvier. “I like the life on the road and visiting these old theater houses across the country. Seeing the locals that I remember and my friends and family that live all over. For me, a transient life is great. Maybe not so great for others. ” Early in his career, he toured with “Phantom of the Opera” for six years. He began in the ensemble and covered two principal roles, and moved to swing which gave him the longevity covering 11 different roles in that show, a life-changing gig that he remembers fondly. WASHINGTON BLADE: As a gay actor touring in a hot musical with some queer themes do you feel that you make an impact? EDWARD JUVIER: Oh yeah, it’s important for queer people to see representation on stage. Our version of the show is a sneak attack; it doesn’t hit you over the head with themes. Seeing an old story that takes a turn where you’re left to accept what’s happening onstage and by that time, you’re in love and rooting with the characters. You feel it from the audiences and we play some of the reddest of states. Queer, trans, nonbinary people meet us at the stage door in tears thanking us for the representation. They didn’t even know when they came to the show that they’re going to see something with such an affirming message to their lives, and they’re thrilled when they find that out. BLADE: How were you drawn into musical theater? JUVIER: I was lucky that my Texas high school made annual trips to New York to see Broadway shows. On one trip, I remember seeing “Will Rogers Follies,” I felt like Keith Carradine was looking and talking right to me. And the next day, we saw “Falsettos,” the original production. After seeing those two very different shows it was as if I blasted off into the Broadway world. BLADE: Did “Falsettos,” a musical about AIDS, resonate with you as young gay student? JUVIER: Absolutely. It shook me to the core. BLADE: Has being gay made you a better actor? JUVIER: I think what makes a great actor is somebody who has enormous empathy, able to put themselves in someone else’s shoes, and what better than a queer artist to be able to empathize. I came out pre- “Will and Grace. ” A different time to be coming out than it is now, which shows immense progress but also put us through challenges. It’s been a part of my journey. I’m lucky to have the best, most supportive family. No Trumpers to deal with when I go home for the holidays. So, I’m grateful for that especially at this time of year. BLADE: How do you approach a comic character like Osgood. JUVIER : I approach him with honesty and simplicity and try to get out of the way of cheap jokes. It’s been with me all my life especially being a queer artist. We grew up watching “Some Like It Hot. ” This takes old themes and jokes that don’t land so well and brings it to a new audience. When the 32-year-old, seemingly respectable woman was charged with the axe murder of her father Andrew and stepmother Abby in the summer of 1892, it sent shock waves across the community and far beyond. In time, the gruesome tale would weave its way into the annals of American crime lore, always remembered through that popular nursery rhyme “Lizzie Borden took an axe, gave her father 40 whacks…” Well, you know the rest. The astoundingly terrific “LIZZIE” (now playing at Keegan Theatre, a short walk from Dupont Circle Metro) builds on the legend. The rock musical with book by Tim Maner, music by Steven Cheslik-deMeyer and Alan Stevens Hewitt, and lyrics by Cheslik-deMeyer and Maner, follows the days leading up to the grisly murders (unseen offstage) through Lizzie’s acquittal, bringing to the fore matters of abuse, oppression, and queer identity. Shrewdly staged and choreographed by Jennifer J. Hopkins, the show begins with a haunting version of “Forty Whacks (Prologue),” featuring the talented cast of four women who can sing, act, move, and deliver the occasional laugh-out-loud line. Clearly, frustrated Lizzie (powerfully played by Caroline Graham) and dominant older sister Emma (Sydne Lyon), both unmarried and still at home, are angsty and deeply unhappy. They resent their father for a litany of reasons including his extreme Yankee frugality. While one of the richest men in Fall River, he chooses to live on a sad street and go without indoor plumbing rather than set up housekeeping in posh digs across town. But it’s when they see Andrew’s great fortune slipping away to their stepmother that their fury reaches new heights. Much of “LIZZIE” takes place at the scene of the crime, the Borden residence – cleverly suggested by scenic designer Josh Sticklin with some clapboard siding, stairways, a bit of period wallpaper and a purposely incongruous, large Borden family coat of arms. Lighting designer Sage Green, convincingly and evocatively, summons at turns a bona fide rock concert experience, dimly lit parlor, or an intimate setting in a small yard. And costume designer Logan Benson savvily adds to the atmosphere. Lizzie’s somber dresses with their accurate to the era leg-of-mutton sleeves give way to something altogether glitzier and more revealing after the murders. There is dialogue, but the Riot Grrrl-inspired work is mostly sung through with punk rock anthems, ballads, and character driven songs. Whether spoken or sung, “LIZZIE” makes no bones about the title character’s guilt while introducing varying levels of collusion among the other women. A knowing wry smirk from the house maid Bridget (Brigid Wallace Harper) says a lot about the family dynamic (“there’s a lock on every door / In every room a prisoner of a long, silent war”) as well as what went down that summer morning at the Borden house. Lizzie’s secret girlfriend Alice (golden throated Savannah Blackwell) who conveniently lives next door, is besotted and watches her every move. Just after the murders, she saw Lizzie burn a dress in the yard. The hard driving score is played by a passionate half-dozen strong band led by Marika Countouris. Sometimes, the instruments overpower the amplified singers and a lyric or two is lost, but that’s not so unusual with rock musicals. At 90 minutes with a leisurely intermission (well-earned by the band and cast, especially Graham as Lizzie who’s onstage throughout, often incorporating frenetic movement and strenuous air guitar into her many songs), the first half explores feelings of entrapment and the second liberation. Despite a shaky alibi, the defendant seems to be winning over the jury. Looks like she might get that grand house on the hill after all. The Borden story has been shared in varied ways including innumerable books and documentaries, Jack Beeson’s opera “Lizzie Borden” (1965), Agnes de Mille’s ballet “Fall River Legend” (1954), and the memorable 1975 TV movie starring Elizabeth Montgomery (best known as the perky reluctant witch Samantha Stevens on TV’s sitcom “Bewitched”) playing against type. Today, the legend endures with “LIZZIE” at Keegan. Courtesy photo Laurie Metcalf and Micah Stock star in “Little Bear Ridge Road.” Julieta Cervantes “Clarkston” was playing at a theater in London. Theodore Paradise Samuel D. Hunter leads a playwriting workshop for high school students in Ketchum. Kirsten Shultz If you’re looking for an especially meandering way to travel between the north central Idaho towns of Troy and Kendrick, one route you could take is Little Bear Ridge Road, a 10-mile journey through rolling hills, countrysides and forests. At the moment, it might be the most famous road in Broadway theater, other than Broadway itself. It’s the setting for “Little Bear Ridge Road,” the long-deferred Broadway debut of Samuel D. Hunter, the Moscow-born playwright who, at age 44, is becoming one of the most admired voices of New York City theater. Along the way, he’s bestowing little moments of big-time pub to the towns, rivers and roadways of his childhood home. The play is about Sarah, an acerbic Idahoan in her 60s who lives near Troy, along the road of the play’s title, and works as a nurse at St. Joseph Regional Medical Center in Lewiston, where, in real life, Hunter’s father, Jay, worked for years as an emergency room physician. Yes, all these places are mentioned in the script. Hunter, who moved to New York City more than two decades ago, wrote the first segment of the play a few years ago while visiting his family’s home, which happens to lie along Little Bear Ridge Road. And he recently returned to NYC from London, where “Clarkston” is being performed as his West End debut at Trafalgar Theater, escorting viewers into a fictional version of that town’s Costco. If your ears are ringing, that’s why. “Little Bear Ridge Road,” an intimate, 95-minute play about Sarah’s reunion with an estranged nephew, opened to critical acclaim and capacity crowds Oct. 30 and will run for 18 weeks at the beautiful, 800-seat Booth Theater in midtown Manhattan. Hunter is riding a burst of pandemic-delayed momentum from “The Whale,” his play adapted into the 2022 film by Darren Aronofsky, who tabbed Hunter as his screenwriter. “The Whale” elicited an Oscar-winning performance from Brendan Fraser. The star of “Little Bear Ridge Road” is Laurie Metcalf, an iconic stage actor whom Greta Gerwig recruited to play the mother in her breakthrough 2017 film, “Lady Bird.” Metcalf and Tony Award-winning director Joe Mantello, neither of whom had met Hunter, approached him two years ago about maybe whipping out a play — it had to be done quickly — that would reignite their long-running association with the Steppenwolf Theater in Chicago. “I couldn’t say no — it was too good an opportunity,” Hunter said in a recent phone interview. “So I said yes, but there was an anxious five months where there was a season announcement on the Steppenwolf website that just said a new play by Sam Hunter starring Laurie Metcalf, directed by Joe Mantello. That’s all it said. So the next five months, I kind of sequestered myself. All I had really told Joe and Laurie was that I had an idea that I was still trying to flesh out that was about watching television. And thankfully that didn’t scare them away.” Five months later, he sent them a draft that drew from his work on Little Bear Ridge Road. They responded immediately, and a workshop was arranged in Chicago. Like, I have a picture of him holding my infant daughter (Frances, now 8 years old).” That production came in the summer of 2024, and the play was transplanted to Broadway last month behind producers Scott Rudin and Barry Diller, maintaining the entire Chicago cast and crew. Over the years, Metcalf developed a habit of handpicking certain lines from a script, sometimes removing the punctuation from them and looking for a slightly different way of interpreting them. This proved OK with Hunter, who is exacting in his stage direction. “With other actors I would be scared, but with Laurie, she knows what she’s doing,” he said. “And I know she knows how to wrangle a line a certain way, and she doesn’t do it all over the place. It’s very selective. “No, she’s really amazing. The thing I really love about Laurie, and the thing I think she really enjoys, is she has this ability to get the biggest laugh imaginable in one line and then, a second later, it’s back to tragedy. It’s kind of an Olympic-level feat. So that’s what I really tried to embrace in writing the character.” One key to securing a producer for the Broadway production was the confidence that Mantello, 62, felt for it and Hunter’s work in general. “His plays are very theatrical,” Mantello told an interviewer, “but I really don’t know how he does it. Even with all this time we’ve spent with him, I don’t actually understand how he does it. It’s a particular kind of quiet genius he has.” Hunter was walking through the lobby of the Booth when a stranger stopped him after one of the early public reviews of the play. “I live on Little Bear Ridge Road,” she said, “and I babysat you once.” It really is a small world after all. At the Booth Theatre, 222 W. 45th St. Actress Laurie Metcalf and playwright Samuel D. Hunter are a match made in Middle America. There are few writers who can sublimely craft, and without any condescension, powerful stories set in flyover country as well as Hunter, whose searing “The Whale” was made into an Oscar-winning movie starring Brendan Fraser . And Metcalf, although a rockstar of the New York stage, still explodes with the ferocious Midwest edge she sharpened for years at Steppenwolf Theatre Company in Chicago. The “Roseanne” actress is never less than nuclear. Both artists, in the best sense, feel like out-of-towners with a lot of punchy truths to lay on the out-of-touch. At the Booth Theatre, Hunter and Metcalf — H&M — have finally teamed up in “Little Bear Ridge Road,” an intimate Pacific-Northwest-set drama about lonely, struggling souls that opened Thursday on Broadway. More From Johnny Oleksinski ‘Eternity’ review: Elizabeth Olsen and Miles Teller star in a rotten rom-com about death ‘Zootopia 2’ review: Disney’s animal kingdom is back in funny, but lesser sequel ‘Wicked’ on Broadway was ripped by critics — and then became a global hit worth billions It’s a hard-hitting, hard-laughing show that combines topics that you arrive at the theater not itching to confront — the COVID pandemic , meth addiction, health insurance, shift pay — into an absorbing story you leave wanting much more of. About the rocky reunion of a strong-minded Idaho aunt who holes up in a distant house in the woods and her 30-something gay nephew, an unsuccessful writer who’s come home after losing his dad, “Little Bear” isn’t so much a living-room play as a Lay-Z-Boy play. A his-and-her’s reclining couch on a wheel of beige carpet is the only scenery, and the estranged pair bond and spar over that most hot-button of subjects: TV shows. You know the fights. Was that series finale pretty good? Or was it the most disappointing hour of television the world has ever experienced? “Game of Thrones,” “Lost,” “Seinfeld,” you name it. 3 Laurie Metcalf and Micah Stock star in “Little Bear Ridge Road” on Broadway. Photo: Julieta Cervantes That’s a more novel idea to explore than you’d think. The theater usually does a fine job of pretending that TV is, at best, a passing fad, when it’s really the national pastime. That’s how people connect now, like it or not — by disconnecting. text: Deadline Print Article deadline-logo-svg Print James Cameron Reveals He “Almost” Directed ‘Wicked’ But “Couldn’t Find The Song” By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Whitney Leavitt & Mark Ballas Share Their ‘Dancing With The Stars’ Freestyle After Elimination, Discuss “Really Heavy” Hate Mail ‘South Park’: Pete Hegseth Deploys Troops Into South Park As Saudi Arabia Sponsors Turkey Trot ‘Stranger Things’ Fans Experience Temporary Netflix Outage As Season 5 Debuts View All November 26, 2025 3:31pm James Cameron reveals he almost directed 'Wicked'. Marc Piasecki/Getty Images/Universal Pictures Although James Cameron has been in his “blue period” since launching the Avatar franchise in 2009, the director is seeing green over what could have been. The 3x Oscar winner revealed he almost took on Wicked movie musical adaptation as he noted that movies have “to be an event” these days for studios to give them big budgets and for audiences to see them in theater. “The kind of movies that I like to watch, let’s say Dune or even Wicked ,” he explained on The Town with Matt Belloni podcast. “I almost made Wicked back when. I really love the story, I mean The Wizard of Oz is one of my favorite [movies]. This is going back 15 years.” Related Stories News ‘Wicked: For Good’s $14.7M Monday Is 2nd Best Ever In November, Top For Non-Holiday YTD News Ariana Grande & Cynthia Erivo Bid Farewell To ‘Wicked’ Roles: “Words Are Not Enough” Confirming he met with Universal Pictures about his take on the 1995 Gregory Maguire book, turned 2003 Broadway musical, Cameron said he “couldn’t find the song” but didn’t totally rule out doing a musical in his career. “I don’t know,” Cameron told Belloni. “Well, my favorite movie is a musical, Wizard of Oz .” Ariana Grande, Jon M. Chu and Cynthia Erivo on the set of ‘Wicked: For Good’ Universal Studios The Titanic writer/director wasn’t the first to attempt to take on Wicked , with Whoopi Goldberg among several actresses who tried to bring the pre-Broadway story to the big screen, with others in consideration being Demi Moore, Claire Danes, Salma Hayek, Laurie Metcalf, Michelle Pfeiffer, Emma Thompson and Nicole Kidman. The story was ultimately adapted into a Tony-winning Broadway musical by Stephen Schwartz and Winnie Holzman, starring Idina Menzel as Elphaba and Kristin Chenoweth as Glinda. Based on the musical and Maguire’s novel, Jon M. Chu’s Wicked: For Good wraps up the story of the Wicked Witch of the West, Elphaba (Cynthia Erivo) and Glinda, the Good Witch (Ariana Grande) years after they first meet at Shiz University and share a life-changing encounter with the Wizard of Oz (Jeff Goldblum). Following last year’s Wicked , the second installment of the feature adaptation has marked a career-best opening for Grande, Erivo and Chu, with a $150M domestic bow and $226M globally. Credit: Marc Piasecki/Getty; Universal Pictures On a recent podcast, James Cameron revealed he was in talks to direct a film version of Wicked . The Avatar and Terminator director ultimately walked away from the opportunity, but doesn't rule out doing a musical movie. Cameron is just the latest Hollywood A-lister to attempt to adapt Gregory Maguire's book or the Broadway production for the big screen. Terminator and Avatar director James Cameron is known for his metallic and his blue creatures, but he almost added green to the mix. While audiences are currently flocking to see Jon M. Chu 's Wicked: For Good , Cameron says he almost directed a Wicked movie around the time he would have been moving on from 2009's Avatar . "I really love the story," the Academy Award winner says on the latest episode of The Town With Matthew Belloni podcast of Wicked , which was first a 1995 novel by Gregory Maguire and then a 2003 Broadway musical starring Kristin Chenoweth and Idina Menzel. Though his love of the characters goes back even further: "I mean, The Wizard of Oz is one of my favorite [movies.]" Cameron confirms he spoke with Universal Pictures execs about taking on the project, which also excited him because he knew it would "be an event," which is what he feels needs to be the case for studios to greenlight the type of budget he is accustomed to working with. But, ultimately, Cameron says he "couldn't find the song." That said, he doesn't rule out a musical movie in his future. Cynthia Erivo and Ariana Grande in 'Wicked'. Giles Keyte/Universal Pictures Cameron is, of course, not the only person who was eager to bring Wicked to the big screen over the years. Producer Marc Platt was president of production at Universal when they first discussed a film version of Maguire's book — before being convinced a Broadway musical was the ideal format to bring the story off the page. "People who had expressed an interest in the first six months included Whoopi Goldberg and Claire Danes ... Salma Hayek had had some interest, and Laurie Metcalf ." As for who should play Glinda, he revealed that "there were a few people top of mind," including Michelle Pfeiffer , Emma Thompson , and Nicole Kidman . "There was kind of a rumble for a minute that [director Robert Zemeckis ] wanted to do it," added Suzanne Todd, who was then an assistant to the producer Joel Silver. But what about Moore? "I think on different days she could do either, but in the moment it was definitely for Elphaba," he said of the actress starring in the film, which he adds was not something she was dead-set on. That said, Maguire had no doubt Moore would make a fantastic choice for his Wicked Witch, saying he could "imagine Demi Moore naked and green on the cover of Vanity Fair " — a reference to her iconic 1991 nude cover for the magazine while seven-months pregnant. Chu’s hit adaptations reached theaters. The revelation sheds new light on the long and winding journey the beloved Broadway musical took to the big screen. Why James Cameron didn’t direct Wicked James Cameron , known for helming films like Titanic and the Avatar franchise, shared that he “almost made Wicked” years ago, confirming that he met with Universal Pictures about adapting Gregory Maguire’s 1995 novel and the hit 2003 Broadway musical. His comments surfaced during The Town with Matthew Belloni podcast , where he discussed why grand-scale storytelling has become the key to securing big theatrical budgets. As Cameron explained, films must increasingly feel like spectacles or “events” for studios to invest heavily in them, something that seemingly drew him to Wicked initially. “The kind of movies that I like to watch, let’s say Dune or even Wicked,” he said. “I almost made Wicked back when. I really love the story, I mean, The Wizard of Oz is one of my favorite [movies]. This is going back 15 years,” Cameron added. However, the project ultimately slipped away. Cameron joked that he “couldn’t find the song,” suggesting that he struggled to fully envision his take on the musical form. Still, he did not dismiss the idea entirely, adding, “I don’t know… Well, my favorite movie is a musical, Wizard of Oz.” His near-involvement shows attempts were made to adapt Wicked before Chu’s version made it to the screen. Across the years, stars like Whoopi Goldberg, Salma Hayek, Nicole Kidman, Emma Thompson, Claire Danes, Lady Gaga, Laurie Metcalf, and Michelle Pfeiffer were linked to various early development efforts. Directors such as J.J. Abrams, Rob Marshall, Ryan Murphy, and others were also reportedly considered. Meanwhile, the Wicked films that did reach audiences have soared commercially. The first installment grossed $758 million worldwide, and Wicked: For Good has earned $253 million globally. It seems to be career highs for stars Cynthia Erivo, Ariana Grande, and director Jon M. Matthew Murphy Share on Facebook Share on X Google Preferred Share to Flipboard Show additional share options Share on LinkedIn Share on Pinterest Share on Reddit Share on Tumblr Share on Whats App Send an Email Print the Article Post a Comment Chess brought in close to $1.9 million across just seven preview performances, positioning the show as one of the top weekly earners in the industry. The Cold War chess musical , starring Lea Michele, Aaron Tveit and Nicholas Christopher, played to close to 100 percent capacity at the Imperial Theatre and grossed $1.86 million, just narrowly coming in behind the mega-hit The Lion King. While reviews have yet to come out (the musical is scheduled to open Nov. 16), this could be quite the turnaround for a show that was an infamous flop when it originally premiered on Broadway in 1988. The average ticket price dropped down to $183.94 from the $208.02 it hit across its first four previews. Related Stories Business Broadway Box Office: 'Harry Potter' Hits Highest Gross Yet With Tom Felton Lifestyle Jonathan Farwell, Unfulfilled Understudy for Yul Brynner on 'The King and I,' Dies at 93 Just in Time , starring Jonathan Groff as singer Bobby Darin, had its highest grossing week yet, hitting $1.38 million across eight performances. The show played to 103 percent capacity at the Circle in the Square Theatre and the average ticket price increased to $241.22. The musical opened at the theater on April 23, 2025 and has been one of the best financially performing musicals of the past year. Hamilton brought in $3.4 million last week, maintaining its spot as the highest weekly grossing show in the industry, followed by Wicked with $2 million, The Lion King with $1.87 million and Chess . Among the new shows, The Queen of Versailles, starring Kristin Chenoweth, upped its tally to $962,332 from just under $900,000 the prior week, as the show jumped to seven performances from six. However, capacity at the St. James Theatre fell slightly to 89 percent from 91 percent. The musical is set to open Nov. 9. Liberation , a new play about a feminist group in the 1970s, opens Tuesday at the James Earl Jones Theatre. The show brought in just under $246,000 last week, in a week that included some comped tickets for press, and played to 68 percent capacity, but will need to up its totals post opening. Little Bear Ridge Road, starring Laurie Metcalf and produced by Scott Rudin, will be the next to open, Thursday, at the Booth Theatre. The new play is faring better with an 87 percent capacity last week, and a gross of $427,910. By Logan Culwell-Block October 30, 2025 BUY TICKETS Laurie Metcalf and Micah Stock in Little Bear Ridge Road Julieta Cervantes The reviews are rolling in for Samuel D. Hunter's Little Bear Ridge Road , which officially opened at the Booth Theatre October 30 after beginning previews October 7. Tony winner Joe Mantello is again directing the new play, which made its world premiere at Chicago's Steppenwolf Theatre last year. The work follows the Fernsby family in rural Idaho as an estranged aunt and nephew reunite following the passing of a family patriarch. Playwright Hunter ( The Whale ) makes his Broadway debut with the work. Also back from that premiere run are stars Laurie Metcalf as Sarah, Micah Stock as Ethan, John Drea as James, and Meighan Gerachis as Paulette. Understudies Jack Ball, Mary Beth Fisher, and Aubie Merrylees round out the company. Casting is by JC Clementz.
